#3490. ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release the film in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

When Siân Heder’s “CODA” premiered at Sundance in 2021 (during the festival’s online-only “pandemic year” and months and months before the film would go on to win Best Picture), it became an early favorite of mine. Mostly, I wrote in my review, though the “drama is marked by familiar beats, its characters bring new dimension to a staid genre.” The same can be said about Heder’s follow-up feature, “Being Heumann,” which brings real life back to the biopic, not only through innumerable compelling characters, but the smart choice to tightly focus this story on one essential moment in the life of the activist Judy Heumann. Related Stories ‘Tender Loving Care’ Trailer: Mike Leigh’s Likely Final Film Pairs Him with a Career-Best Kate O’Flynn ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

When we first meet Judy (Ruth Madeley in a true star turn), she’s zipping along a busy New York City street in 1972. That might sound fun, but for Judy, it’s just the way things are; a wheelchair user since she was just a toddler (thanks to an early bout with polio), the world is not made for people like Judy, and she makes her way through it however she can. Often, that means doing things like, oh, zipping down city streets, because there are no curb cuts to assist her in smoothly moving from sidewalk to sidewalk. As Judy goes barreling down the street, people stare, drivers yell, and the brassy Brooklynite throws up a finger.

That Judy has natural presence is a given, but the central question of Heder’s film — which she adapted from Heumann’s autobiography alongside co-writer Rebekah Taussig — is how she will use all that verve to truly enact change. It’s the sort of concern that has always impacted great leaders, and suffice it to say, Heumann was indeed a great leader. But while Heumann’s long, storied life had many incredible chapters (she passed away in 2023, two years after she started working with Heder on the film), the filmmakers smartly zero in one on seminal slice of life to craft “Being Heumann.” Cradle to the grave this is not, but the film still succeeds mightily when contextualizing Heumann’s role in the disability rights movement and her singularity as a true American original.

That’s not to say that the period of time covered by the film — which soon jumps ahead five years — isn’t complicated and dense. The film opens in 1972, because that’s when Judy and eighty other activists staged a sit-in on Madison Avenue to protest the vetoing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which we’re told was one of the very first pieces of federal legislation meant to guarantee certain rights to people with disabilities (from accessibility to education). The act was eventually signed in 1973, but when the film picks back up in 1978, it has not been implemented. It needed one last step: a signature from newly-installed Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo). And he wasn’t signing.

Heder and Taussig’s script distills the legal wrangling down well: this piece of legislation will help bring about massive positive change for the disabled community, but it will cost a lot of money, and Califano has already been asked to slash the budget. These are excellent stakes.

Judy doesn’t care about the cost to the government — why should she? — but she does care about the cost to her community. A seasoned and dogged activist, most of the people in Judy’s life are disabled in some way, and it’s her mission to a) wrangle them into action and b) be pretty pushy about it. Heder and her casting directors Bernard Telsey and Adam Caldwell have assembled a wonderful, winning cast around Madeley (herself a wheelchair user), including a number of disabled performers, cast here as icons in their own right. Standouts include Madeline Delp as Kitty Cone (the honey to Judy’s vinegar), Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, Antwan Tolliver as Brad Lomax, “CODA” star Daniel Durant as Steve McCleeland, Roberta Colindrez as Joni Breves, and instant star Charlie Rush-Reese as Dennis Billups.

That Heder would cast actually disabled people in these roles should seem obvious (this is the filmmaker behind “CODA,” after all), but there’s no question that it totally pays off all the same. The wide array of performers on offer here is thrilling, and it’s a treat to see them all settling in so well to this period world, rendered tactile and realistic by smart costuming choices by Danny Glicker and unfussy production design by John P. Goldsmith.

Enraged over the lack of movement on the signing of 504, Judy and her compatriots launch a series of protests around the country, focused on federal buildings that house HEW offices. Califano, stuck back in DC, can only hear about these events as they unfold, utterly stymied but what to do, paralyzed by fear for his job, and intent on reminding people he’s one of the good guys (he supported the Selma marches!). But the world has changed. When Judy somewhat impulsively leads a pack of protesters inside the SF federal building, what follows will only spark further change.

Despite the historical implications that follow — the SF sit-in became one of the country’s largest — Heder doesn’t noodle on the cultural vegetable aspect of this story. Instead, “Being Heumann” becomes something unexpectedly frisky and fun. The sit-in comes with plenty of challenges (beyond the myriad needs of the disabled community, there’s in-fighting to spare, government pressures galore, and deep worries about how it might actually pan out), but there’s also a streak of joy that runs through it. It’s thrilling to see people doing literally whatever they can for their well-being, and having a good time in the process (yes, you’ll get acquainted with their “sex tents” soon enough). There are almost too many colorful characters here, a sprawling ensemble in which everyone deserves their own film, though we occasionally lose some threads along the way.

That isn’t always easy for Judy, though, who remains set in her ways even as she sees real change happening around her. Madeley captures the real Judy Heumann’s energy beautifully; she’s funny and flinty and spiky and smarter than anyone else around her and totally driven by her sense of justice and equality. But that’s not always enough, a lesson that “Being Heumann” is not shy about. Fighting for what’s right involves just that, fighting. Sometimes, that even means fighting your own instincts.

A film like ”Being Heumann” is destined to be called rousing — a call to action that’s every bit as entertaining as it is inspiring. It’s a film about tough choices and even tougher circumstances, but it’s also about the tangible good that can come from people working together. What could be more joyous than that? More biopics could learn from this formula, and from this feeling. Be more like Judy: be tough, but never be afraid of joy.

“Being Heumann” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

#3489. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3487. ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Ask any gay man with a social media account, and they likely have an opinion about Jordan Firstman. The backlash-courting queer actor/comedian, controversial most recently because of an online flare-up over querying the sexual realism of “Heated Rivalry,” is labeled either candid or confrontational. He also has a record of taking on sexually explicit projects like Sebastian Silva’s suicide-ideating, ketamine-fueled dark comedy “Rotting in the Sun.” His status as a self-aware, hyper-online provocateur may not seem to suggest the makings of a bona fide filmmaker, but just wait. Related Stories ‘Tender Loving Care’ Trailer: Mike Leigh’s Likely Final Film Pairs Him with a Career-Best Kate O’Flynn ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

While that reputation might have Firstman on guard as he debuts his feature writing/directing debut “Club Kid,” as it will certain circumspect corners of the audience, this terrific movie should put any of those nervous feelings to rest. Even his haters won’t be able to resist what’s announced here as a major filmmaking talent with a sensitive side that belies his brash, internet-based persona.

He also stars as the protagonist of his hugely crowd-pleasing, excruciatingly funny, and poignant first film — one that plays to all sides of the room despite being brazenly, unapologetically queer — which will prime Firstman-savvy viewers to immediately interpret “Club Kid” as autobiographical. That’s because it is.

He plays party promoter Peter, now in his thirties after a decade-plus of MDMA-addled revelry, the kind where all the days blur and blot into one long and sweaty night with a coming horizon in the shape of regret. Firstman may not be playing himself this time, but he is playing a version of that self, having, as he says, spent enough years in Berlin to be labeled “the angel of Berghain” by his new friends, but now ready to put the days-that-became-years of GHB, MDMA, and other letters of the alphabet behind him.

“Club Kid” is exactly about what happens when the lights go up on the party, the shameover of the morning after that becomes a way of being, and the need to do it all over again to stave off last night’s aching after effects. But it’s also about — earnesty alert! — family lost and found, not only because of the queer community formed around the now-orphaned Peter, who lives in the rent-controlled Manhattan his mother left him after she died, but because he wakes up one day to find a child he fathered and never knew about, literally on his doorstep.

“Club Kid” was shot on 35mm on location in New York City with a team of backers including “Anora” Oscar-winning producer Alex Coco and nepo filmmaker Olmo Schnabel, and a millennial cast of queer comedians. So it’s hard not to leave the movie thinking all that’s needed here is an A24 logo slapped onto the opening credits, and it’s ready for the world. But no matter; while Firstman’s aesthetic is loudly in A24’s register, it turns out to be an asset rather than a limitation.

Beginning inside a sensually lit, drug-soaked party and ending as one rages on without you from afar, “Club Kid” drops us into Brooklyn 2016. Peter, sing-screaming Rihanna’s “Sex with Me” in a clown car of an Uber ride with his friends, is headed into yet another bender to remember (but also eventually forget). At a club of the sort that now dominates night culture in Bushwick, rising party promoter Peter ends up hooking up — and then really hooking up — with a couple of hyperactive “innit, babes?” British women in the back room. It’s all inconspicuously taking a turn for the sexual when the movie smash cuts to “a decade or so later,” when the proverbial party is still dying down, but Peter is still living in it — albeit more sweaty and tragic 10 years on.

He’s now made a career out of his drug use with his best friend and business partner Sophie (a marvelous, perpetually coked-out Cara Delevingne, who’s two inches from a breakdown at all times). A few days before the one that’s about to change his life, they have an important sit-down coming up with FiDi investors to help expand their New York party empire. But alas, as he couldn’t help himself once again the night before, Peter wakes up drugged to the gills, rushing to the meeting only to nod off at the table, still in a GHB-spiked stupor. (His reaction to a dropper of hot sauce that looks curiously similar to the one he used last night to get high is one of the film’s many brilliantly funny little pratfalls.)

All of that’s to say Peter’s life is still totally a mess, and his arrested development from a decade of partying has now washed him out to the point where sobriety is maybe never part of his day. (A weekend spent dissipated, hungover, jerking off to internet porn and eating Popeye’s in bed rings painfully true.)

Party’s certainly over, though, when one of those British “innit babes” from 10 years ago, Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), shows up from London at his apartment (where Peter lives with an “Azerbaijanian aspiring queer philosopher” who doesn’t pay rent) with an eight-year-old boy. “You’ve got a kid! ‘Yay!,’” she tells him while delivering the news that Arlo (preternaturally gifted young breakout actor Reggie Absalom) is in fact Peter’s child with one of the other women from that opening-scene heterosexual encounter, who’s just died. The first and only time Peter fucked a woman, and now he’s fucked himself into having to finish raising a small boy.

Cue the manic panic, more drug use, and resignation to the idea that there’s no sending this kid back to the U.K.

While it’s a bit sudden how fast the switch flips from Peter feeling wildly ill-equipped for parenting to becoming a nurturing caretaker, he and Arlo turn out to have more in common than not. Arlo, for one, has the music taste of someone who grew up on Pitchfork, eagerly taking to the $300 Elliott Smith record Peter buys for him in a later scene. (The soundtrack on this thing, by the way, rules, from Arthur Russell during the film’s melancholy final act to “The White Lotus” composer Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s deeply felt original score.) Their relationship, however quickly, becomes the film’s so-far unexpected sweet center, as Peter starts to really appreciate and eventually love Arlo, who has traumas of his own.

A lot of the success of “Club Kid” rides not only on Firstman’s shoulders, but also on the collaborators he’s working with, including cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra who captures a certain lost-era grit in New York as well as in the chaos-packed nightclub sequences. “Club Kid” also takes advantage of New York City as not just a backdrop but a central character in the storytelling, using the city in a way that feels rare onscreen these days.

“Club Kid” freewheels and unwinds like a head rush of a zippy party movie until Arlo’s introduction brings the comedown. It turns out he feels more at home among Peter’s “found family” of queer revelers, discovering his own DJ skills in the process, than he ever did in London. Could Peter really warm to fatherhood? Real emotional stakes start to heighten as he begins recognizing the unexpected realities of his new arrangement, like getting Arlo into school, or keeping the boy shielded from the drug use of his friends while Peter’s own finally starts to diminish. A nervous, tentative romance comes into view with child psychologist Oscar (Diego Calva), and on a date where a namecheck of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin” becomes not just a tender confession, but a turn-on.

“Club Kid” takes a sharp dramatic turn, in which the nature of Arlo’s living situation becomes even more dire and probably illegal, that almost shouldn’t work in a comedy like this — but it’s a turn that feels inevitable given how “Club Kid” is structured like the rise and fall of a drug experience, a high that crashes down into despair. The emotional arc bends toward “Kramer vs. Kramer” territory with a cathartic (and well-played by Firstman) courtroom oner. Peter may be insecure about his own place in a world where only parts of it have room for him, but as a storyteller with an eye, Firstman is anything but.

Firstman is by now an established comedic voice, but his work on all sides of the camera here leaves pretty of room for revelation, for him to become a genuine discovery beyond an audience of gay, internet-addled millennials. “Club Kid” has real potential to break out bigger than its seemingly niche scope would suggest, with Firstman finally shirking the ironic pose he’s taken online for years to emerge as a sincere storyteller with heart as much as humor.

“Club Kid” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3485. 9 Fantasy Shows That Rival Lord of the Rings

The Lord of the Rings may be the poster child of fantasy, but other works can also give the epic masterpiece a run for its money. J.R.R. Tolkien's legendary story follows Frodo Baggins as he inherits the One Ring and sets out to destroy it, saving Middle-earth and its inhabitants in the process. The Lord of the Rings has told plenty of stories about heroes, villains, and saving the world from doom, but fantasy shows have found their own ways to explore those same big ideas.

Some have taken things a step further by breaking away from the usual good-versus-evil divide, showing how fantasy can be a lot closer to home than we realize, or proving that a story doesn't need to be grand in scale to be great. From a fight for the Iron Throne to an adventure across the Grand Line, here are the fantasy shows that rival The Lord of the Rings.

The Witcher demystifies what it means to be a hero. One might think that being a monster hunter would make Geralt of Rivia (Henry Cavill and Liam Hemsworth) a noble figure in the eyes of villagers. However, his title and powers often do him more harm than good. To those who fear him, he's a monster; to those with money, he's simply useful.

Unlike The Lord of the Rings, which relies on a more traditional distinction between good and evil, The Witcher embraces moral ambiguity. Its morally complex characters aren't just for show; they portray how good and evil constantly overlap. Even the noblest intentions can cause harm, while the most wicked people may still have a shred of integrity.

Everything is political, including fantasy shows. For all of Game of Thrones' imagined realms and treacherous dragons, much of the show revolves around the pursuit of political power. Unlike The Lord of the Rings, where the central conflict is about destroying the One Ring and preventing its power from falling into the wrong hands, Game of Thrones focuses on the very human struggle to claim the throne.

This is a huge reason why Game of Thrones appeals even to non-fantasy watchers. The show explores the mechanics of gaining power, revealing the tactics and strategies people use to get there. In the process, it exposes the deeply human strengths and flaws of its characters, often leading to some of television's most shocking betrayals and plot twists.

At its heart, One Piece is a coming-of-age story about growing together, except that they’re on a ship in the middle of the sea. Despite coming from different worlds, One Piece shares one thing in common with The Lord of the Rings: both feature their own ragtag teams. Instead of the Fellowship, One Piece has the equally eccentric Straw Hat crew.

Unlike the Fellowship, which eventually breaks apart, the Straw Hats remain together throughout their pirate adventures. Each member brings something different to the crew, playing an important role aboard the ship and in the story's emotional arcs. Their relationships also shape how they grow as individuals, making One Piece more than just a fantasy adventure.

The Lord of the Rings wowed fans with its grandiose, epic fantasy, but Merlin proves that "common," everyday magic can be just as intriguing. Sure, there's destiny, royalty, and marvelous creatures, but Merlin also knows how to have fun with its ridiculous shenanigans, which is a true ode to the fantasy genre itself.

Think getting possessed by a goblin or briefly marrying a troll. Merlin knows when to take a cheeky breather between all the spectacle. While it's based on Arthurian legend, the show isn't strict about following canon. It allows its characters to grow, change, and fall from grace, showing that the only way to fulfill one's prophecy is to allow oneself to evolve when circumstances call for it.

Season 2 may have its pacing issues, but it's hard not to give The Sandman its flowers for changing the fantasy landscape on streaming. Rather than telling a story from one perspective, as is the case with Frodo, The Sandman gives individual episodes room to tell their own stories while contributing to Morpheus' (Tom Sturridge) larger journey.

This allows the show to experiment with its storytelling while maintaining its central quest. Thanks to this experimentation, The Sandman isn't confined to traditional fantasy norms. Whether it's a story about freeing a former lover from an author or a serial-killer storyline, the series meshes horror, drama, and mythology into a darker, grittier fantasy setting, making it all the more of a shame that the show was canceled so abruptly.

Unlike The Lord of the Rings and its traditional high-fantasy beliefs, where heroes generally represent the forces of good, Castlevania twists the genre with a bloodier, morally complicated story in which even the villains have a point. This beautifully hand-drawn, anime-inspired take on Dracula wants audiences to sympathize with characters who are otherwise canonically evil.

Set in 15th-century Wallachia, the Gothic fantasy initially presents Dracula as a bloodthirsty murderer, only to reveal that his crusade against humanity comes from profound grief rather than simple vengeance. The series makes righteousness a debatable concept, questioning whether institutions that preach morality actually practice what they preach, while suggesting that those who endure the greatest suffering may have the clearest understanding of humanity.

His Dark Materials isn't afraid to get philosophical, downright uncomfortable, and, some might say, dangerously close to blasphemous. While The Lord of the Rings explores good and evil through opposing, supernatural forces, His Dark Materials gives these ideas a more concrete form through corrupt institutions inspired by religious establishments. These institutions claim to uphold righteousness but resort to cruel methods, sacrificing innocent lives for their so-called greater good.

What begins as a child's adventure quickly becomes something much bigger as Lyra gets caught between curious scholars and an authoritarian religious institution. Armored polar bears, talking spirit animals, and parallel universes share the screen with religious persecution, Original Sin, and a prophecy about a new Eve—adding layer after layer to this complex but tightly written fantasy series.

Right from the get-go, Avatar: The Last Airbender excels at something The Lord of the Rings couldn't do: putting a group of children at the center of its story. There's something earnest and painfully honest about watching children forced to grow up in war-torn nations, especially when they're tasked with saving them.

In a world ruled by four elements, Aang must fulfill his destiny as the Avatar, but he can't do it without his newfound friends. Throughout three seasons, this crew faces hardships, sacrifices, and losses that even adults would struggle to handle. But Avatar isn't just about becoming the strongest warrior. It's also about breaking free from others' expectations, challenging prophecies, and finding the courage to forge our own paths.

The Lord of the Rings will forever be timeless, but younger generations of fantasy enthusiasts are looking for something more modern and relatable. Look no further than Percy Jackson and the Olympians. The 2010s movie adaptations ignited interest in Rick Riordan's books, and the latest television adaptation does the story even more justice by taking it further through its episodic format.

It's classic Greek mythology with a modern-day makeover, giving it a more approachable feel to even non-fantasy viewers. While the story revolves around celestial, supernatural battles, Percy Jackson and the Olympians is ultimately about young kids trying to find their place in a world where their parents are worshiped as gods.

12-year-old modern demigod, Percy Jackson, is coming to terms with his newfound divine powers when the sky god, Zeus, accuses him of stealing his master lightning bolt; with his friend's help, Percy must restore order to Olympus.

#3484. ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Many scenes in “Wildwood” are designed to look spectacular. Even if each frame weren’t already rendered with the meticulous detail and artistry of stop-motion animation, the Laika Studios film is full of complex, chaotic battle sequences, a forest writhing with eldritch magic, and giant eagles soaring through the sky.

But some of the most technically challenging scenes, according to director Travis Knight, aren’t the ones that look the most majestic. They are — true to the spirit of the film and the lesson learned by its stubborn, caring protagonist Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) — the simple magic of everyday life. Related Stories ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

In fact, Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast that one of the most challenging sequences in “Wildwood” was simply getting its hero from one end of her bedroom to the other. Laika prefers Canon cameras mounted on large motion-control rigs, which offer the flexibility needed to capture puppet movements adjusted one frame at a time. But when the camera moves, it also has to do so one painstaking frame at a time.

Knight, who’s now directed live-action features “Bumblebee” and “Masters of the Universe” in addition to his Laika work on “Kubo and the Two Strings,” wanted “Wildwood” to have the same camera language as a live-action film. He wanted the intimacy and wordless visual storytelling of a camera tracking Prue as she huffs across her bedroom, where the camera movement helps us see the decor shift from the artifacts of a carefree kid to those of a more disaffected teen.

“I still wanted it to feel like it was shot like a live-action film, with that kind of intimacy with the camera. But a camera on a motion-control rig is the size of a Ford F-150 in our [puppet-scale] world. It’s huge. And so if a camera is moving, you have to create space for the camera on set,” Knight said.

This is on top of creating space for the animator, who is roughly the size of a Kaiju in comparison to the fifth-scale the humans on either side of the Impassable Wood live at. The Prue puppet is roughly 10 inches tall. Being able to move that puppet and a camera at least as large as her bedroom that the puppet is moving through? That is a particularly gnarly feat of physics.

“We essentially had to deconstruct the set,” Knight said. “It was almost like it was a clamshell. It would open to make room for the camera, and then it would close up again. It was such a complicated engineering feat, when all it is [for] is a camera panning across a room. Those are the kinds of challenges that the team has to figure out, which is stupid, but it’s what it requires if you’re trying to tell a story like this.”

There is much to be said, and rightly, about the awe-inducing moments of spectacle in “Wildwood.” The Laika team had to figure out how to make giant puppets out of fabric and feathers instead of standard-issue silicone to simulate flight compellingly, accurately, and tactilely. Combat sequences required enormous attention to detail. But when Knight watches the film, he’s just as struck by the invisible work that makes “Wildwood” feel like a live-action epic — the thankless but involving work that viewers aren’t ever meant to see.

“I learned a great many things about what to do, what not to do [working in live-action]. It fundamentally changed my relationship with the camera, which is one of the reasons why ‘Wildwood’ looks so different. It’s because I wanted it to feel as if it were without the inherent limitations you would typically find in stop-motion cinematography,” Knight said. “When I see this movie, I am seeing all these little miraculous moments of engineering and artistry and human creativity at play on the big screen, and that’s one of the reasons it moves me so much.”

#3480. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

Freestyle Digital Media, the digital film distribution division of Byron Allen’s company Allen Media Group, has acquired VOD rights to the documentary feature “The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan.”

The documentary follows Oscar-nominated and Emmy-winning actor Gary Sinise‘s decades-long mission to honor America’s fighting men and women, support injured veterans, and stand beside Gold Star families. It’s a calling that was inspired by Sinise’s work playing a Vietnam vet in “Forrest Gump.”

“The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan” will be available on North American digital HD internet, DVD, cable, and satellite platforms starting on November 10, 2026. It features interviews with Sinise, as well as Jay Leno, Tim Allen, Joe Mantegna, Chip Foose, and Mykelti Williamson. Sinise is also known for his work in films such as “Ransom” and “Apollo 13,” as well as the TV series “CSI: NY.” He starred in “George Wallace,” winning an Emmy. Related Stories ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

The film also follows Sinise as he grapples with personal tragedy after his son, Mac, dies of cancer at the age of 33. The documentary looks at how Sinise is motivated by the credo: “We can always do a little more.” “The Ballad of Lieutentant Dan” was directed by Steve Mitchell Beebe and produced by Bud Brutsman.

“’The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan’ looks into the world of actor and humanitarian, Gary Sinise, and explores how his commitment to veterans and first responders created a community that supported him through a difficult period in his life,” said Beebe. “This is a story about selfless kindness and, I hope, will inspire all of us to do what we each can to uplift our friends, neighbors and communities.”

Freestyle Digital Media negotiated a deal to acquire the documentary directly with the filmmakers.

#3477. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

#3476. Only 3 Movies Are More Entertaining Than The Lord of the Rings

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

The Lord of the Rings showed us how incredible it feels to follow characters through a massive adventure. We watched them grow through every danger, sacrifice, and impossible decision in three films. But some movies manage to deliver that same rush in just a couple of hours. They pull you into situations so intense that you almost forget you're watching a film. You find yourself holding your breath during a chase, worrying about someone you've only known for an hour, or desperately hoping a character makes the right choice before everything falls apart.

What makes the three films on this list unforgettable is how deeply grounded their stakes remain in human emotion. They prove that when a movie respects its characters' choices and allows their relationships to evolve naturally, even in the middle of total chaos, the audience stays entirely hooked. Their victories feel earned. Their sacrifices linger. Let's look at how these three films pull it off.

Raiders of the Lost Ark is fun because Indiana Jones (Harrison Ford) can be brilliant, frightened, stubborn, and unlucky within the same minute. In the opening temple, he measures the sand, swaps the idol for a bag of sand, and still loses the prize when the mechanism starts closing. Then he runs from a giant boulder and loses the idol to Belloq (Paul Freeman). Indy can know exactly what he’s doing and still find himself in a worse situation.

The map room is a pleasure, as Indy uses the staff and sunlight to locate the Ark while the Nazis do the digging for him. But the film keeps its people in view, too. Marion (Karen Allen) survives captivity, tries to drink Belloq under the table, and refuses to cooperate. When the Ark opens, Indy tells Marion to shut her eyes and holds her close. The movie fittingly ends its wildest spectacle with Indy protecting her.

Terminator 2: Judgment Day begins with a brilliant reversal. The machine that tried to kill Sarah (Linda Hamilton) in the first film is now walking toward John (Edward Furlong), while the new T-1000 (Robert Patrick) is hunting him. At the mall, John has to decide whether to trust either one. His order that the Terminator (Arnold Schwarzenegger) must not kill anyone becomes the first boundary John sets with the machine.

Sarah’s escape from Pescadero is the film’s hardest moment. She reaches Miles Dyson (Joe Morton) with a gun, sees his children, and cannot make herself shoot him. That hesitation gives John and the Terminator time to arrive, and the machine helps Dyson understand what his research will cause. The chases and gunfights are spectacular, but the true core of the movie is the machine learning that a promise matters. It refuses to kill, comforts John, and finally lowers itself into the molten steel because it understands why it must go. John’s face as the Terminator gives him the thumbs-up is heartbreaking. The machine has changed. It understands love. It learns how to say goodbye.

Mad Max: Fury Road keeps changing the rescue as the characters learn what it will cost. The story follows Furiosa (Charlize Theron), who smuggles the Five Wives out of the Citadel, and Max (Tom Hardy), who is chained to Nux’s (Nicholas Hoult) car as a blood bag when the pursuit begins. The pursuit is packed with detail at every turn. You see the War Rig, the Pole Cats swinging between vehicles, Nux trying to earn Immortan Joe’s (Hugh Keays-Byrne) approval, and Furiosa protecting the women without stopping to explain herself.

Then the plan changes. The Green Place is gone, so Furiosa and the others must turn back through the army chasing them. Furiosa finally faces Joe, and the chase ends with his death and his followers’ defeat. On the return, the Wives open the water gates and the Citadel’s people rise to meet them. The ending gives each victory a visible result. Joe is dead, Furiosa is carried upward, and water reaches people who were denied it, leaving a sense of exhilaration and relief for all involved.

#3475. Watch ‘The Greatest’ Team Discuss How They Made the Impossible ‘Possible’ on Muhammad Ali Series

As tall an order as it was to make a series about the greatest boxer of all time, “The Greatest” creator Ben Watkins had faith he assembled the right team for the job and the unique assurance of making it with the blessing of Muhammed Ali’s family. At IndieWire’s recent Consider This event at Pacific Design Center, presented in partnership with Prime Video, he broke down the process that brought the series to life.

“One of the things I want to do is humanize Muhammad Ali because everybody sort of pictures him as a fully formed icon and legend. And I want to disconnect people from that and introduce them to a kid who just had a dream. But that means I got to show all of him. I got to show flaws and fears and vulnerabilities and tell the truth like that. And it’s sometimes messy,” Watkins said, recalling his pitch to the boxer’s widow Lonnie Ali . “Her response was, ‘That’s what I want too,’ because that will make him more relatable. And as we introduce him to a younger generation and reintroduce him to the people who already love him, that is what will make this story fresh.” Related Stories Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again ‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself

Boxing is an individual sport, but making “The Greatest” was a team effort. Watkins was joined on the panel by many of his crafts team members, including editor Steve Lang, costume designer Marci Rodgers, production designer Elisa Suavé, composer Stanley A. Smith, music editor Jordan Wiggins, and music supervisor Robin Urdang.

One of the aspects that made the eight-episode limited series tracking the protagonist’s rise from Olympian gold medalist Cassius Clay to heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali feel fresh was the use of contemporary music, but that also came with its own challenges for the post production team.

“Going contemporary in an Olympic boxing match with so many things going on between commentary, the fight itself, the reactions, and then we also have a song playing. I think we went through about 120 songs,” said Lang, telling the story of how they landed on a key piece of music for the series opener.

“I usually come on pre-production, [but] I came on during post, and one of the first things was ‘We want an original song here and we need it now,’” Urdang added. “I said, ‘We can’t get it until we create the sound of the show because there’s no sound of the show right now.’”

That first music cue became the last song they used for the show, an original track from Grammy winner Wyclef Jean titled “Gladiator.” “There was a poem that [Ali] hears about a gladiator talking about his time in the Colosseum. Ben mentions that to Wyclef, who then takes those lyrics and turns them into the song that you hear during that fight,” said Lang.

“It ended up in two spots in episode one, and then it also became the main title [music],” said Wiggins. “It was a lot of cutting that Jordan did for us,” said Urdang.

The Colosseum also happened to be the setting for one of costume designer Marci Rodgers’ greatest challenges working on “The Greatest.” “I was put on the spot in Rome where I had to do a quick change on camera, which is actually the first scene [as well]” she said. “So we’re in the Colosseum and it’s Marci’s time. And so I reached out to one of my mentors, Paul Tazewell, who walked me through a process in which we see essentially his suit removed as the camera is moving around.”

“Those are the things that they said would not be possible. Then the first production meeting I said, ‘Hey, I want to do a shot where he’s in a suit and as we’re circling, it all goes away,’” said Watkins. First it was a challenge to even shoot on location, but “We ended up [as] the first television show to ever shoot in the Colosseum,” he said. Then it was getting confirmation that they could also shoot more around Rome. And finally, it was shooting the aforementioned pivotal scene. “At that point I said, ‘We’ll never get that shot off.’ And then Marci says, ‘No, we’re going to figure out a way to build a suit, to do it in a way to get the shot off.’ And then Elisa and her team figured out a way for us to not just be able to shoot in the Colosseum, but they recreated a 60s-level Italian neighborhood because, ‘Hey, we’re in Rome now, so let’s get the most out of it.’ And they got us all of that, all things they said they couldn’t get.”

For her part, Suavé said “When you look at the world in the ’50s and the ’60s, there was no digital anything. Every single sign, every single thing you think was made by our scenic artists by hand, not with projections that they were copying. We did it all by hand. We made all the molds for all the parking meters. We made the molds and we created the gold medals.” She added, “There was not one world that we didn’t touch or create.”

Composer Stanley A. Smith also chimed in on how the series kept things analog, saying “We use all live musicians in this score.” “No AI,” added Urdang.

“Ben was really great about going to bat for getting the budget to do that. And we used live string players.” said Smith. “Just because of the nature of the tone we wanted, we used predominantly people of color for our strings — not always — but because we wanted that feel. And actually, I’m going to go one step further. It was 60 to 40 percent female.”

Ending the panel, Watkins said “That’s the big testament to everybody up here. We took what I would say is a modest television budget and we made a high budget film.”

“The Greatest” is now streaming on Prime Video. Watch the complete panel with the showrunner and artisans who worked on the limited series in the video above.

#3474. Early Look At The Mighty Nein's Return In Brand New Critical-Role Story

Critical Role has delivered no shortage of beloved actual play seasons, from its Vox Machina origins to the iconic Mighty Nein, and these stories live on beyond the show itself. From animated TV series to tie-in novels, Critical Role's world of Exandria has expanded into its own universe of stories. And another new story set in the Critical Role universe is headed our way very soon.

Caleb Widogast and Beauregard Lionett of The Mighty Nein will return this month in a brand-new official sequel novel. Critical Role: The Mighty Nein: Children of Empire arrives on November 10, bringing fans back ot Wildemount for a new, first-of-its-kind official sequel to Critical Role's Mighty Nein campaign. The story, written by award-winning author Nibedita Sen, bridges the gap between Campaign 2 and Campaign 3, Bells Hells.

ScreenRant has the pleasure of presenting fans with an exclusive excerpt of the upcoming Critical Role novel. In this sneak peek of the new adventure ahead, we find Caleb Widogast and Beau Linnett hiking Mount Mentiri.

You can pre-order Critical Role: The Mighty Nein - Children of Empire here.

Mud sucks greedily at the soles of Beau’s boots as she strides up the mountain toward her family’s vineyard. They pass the great wooden bas­ket presses, which are silent now but will later serenade the hills with their creaking, cranking song. She guides them through rows of trellises burdened with dusk-and-ruby grapes, deftly hopscotching along the strips of headland that cut the crop into blocks. The air is thick with bruised skins and spilt juice.

Workers move among the rows, de-stemming grapes and filling wicker baskets for the crushers. A few acknowledge her with a tip of the chin or a touch to the brim of a straw hat, and Beau raises a hand in re­turn.

The vineyard didn’t go under after the Crownsguard marched her father off to jail, but it was a near thing. Thoreau Lionett, lifelong para­noiac, never believed in delegating. Beau was the only person he ever taught to read his ledgers, and she wasn’t around for the aftermath of his arrest. Paydays were missed. Rich clients in Deastok got wind of the scandal and canceled orders. People quit. Beau suspects the Stassmans poached more than a few of them, seizing this opportunity to seduce their rival’s staff.

She could have helped, if she’d been here. She could have done what her father had been training her to do. But she’d been walking the dusty wastes of Xhorhas with Yasha to find Zuala’s grave, and after that, help­ing the Cobalt Soul put together their case against Trent Ikithon. By the time she mustered the willpower to hop on a carriage back to Kamordah, the vineyard was in a death spiral, hollowed out by wartime tax rates and an overseer who was taking advantage of her mother’s bewilderment to brazenly line his own pockets.

Beau absently cracks her knuckles at the memory. She and Yasha had, ah, persuaded the man to seek a change of career. Maybe even a change of location. They must have been pretty convincing too, ’cause he was on a cart out of town the very next day.

The sun is hot on the nape of her neck. The uphill trek is nothing for her strong calves, fed on a diet of lengthy morning runs and fifty crunches before breakfast. Caleb, on the other hand, is breathing hard.

“Beauregard,” he manages, Zemnian accent gone extra gravelly with exertion. “Would you like perhaps for me to transport us to our destina­tion? If you will only describe it to me, I will gladly make the attempt.”

“C’mon, it won’t hurt you to sweat a little. I’ve been climbing this mountain since I learned to walk.”

She hears him sigh. “Eluding capture,” Caleb says. “For now. We thought it best he not stay in one place too long.”

“Still comes by to see you, though, huh?” Beau twists to glance back at him. She waggles an eyebrow with wicked glee. Caleb coughs.

“Yes, well,” he says awkwardly. “We enjoy each other’s company.”

She smirks to herself. “Oh, I bet you do.”

They continue to climb, crossing the terraces carved into the rolling chromatic hills. Beau can’t help but catalog every yellowed leaf and bowed rung she passes. They’re behind schedule. The first crop of purple cinder should already be macerating by this point in the season. The ice thistles will be rotting on the vine. They could try to dry some—even straw wine’s better than no wine—but they just don’t have the man­power.

She doesn’t want to see it. What’s the point in seeing problems she can’t fix? The vineyard’s not her responsibility anymore. Her old man made that real clear.

But before she became his misfortune, she was his heir. He taught her too well, and old lessons die hard. How to tell root rot from leaf blight; how to taste the difference between an oak barrel and a chestnut one. How to balance the books and make the numbers sing a good song. All the things she could and should have done instead of leaving the vineyard in the lurch when it needed her most.

This was all supposed to be hers someday. Still could be, if she felt like fighting a toddler for it.

“Your father will be a free man next month,” Caleb says.

He remembered. Of course he fucking remembered, it’s what he does, and he was right there beside her in the courtroom when the sen­tence was passed. Beau shoves her hands into the pockets of her loose pants and keeps walking. “Uh-huh.”

“Fuck no. I’m just checking on my mom. Making sure she didn’t freak out and run off to her parents or get swindled into selling the whole vineyard to a Marquesian prince. We were gonna be out of here before he gets back.”

And now she has a great excuse to cut the visit short. Sorry, Mom, duty calls. Gotta go save the Empire from itself. She can pack her bags, grab her girlfriend, and get out of this place where her own skin doesn’t fit right. Like she’s been stuffed back into something she’s outgrown and must tread carefully for fear of splitting her seams and spilling guts ev­erywhere.

The thought cheers her. Then Caleb sours her mood again by saying, very softly, “She must be glad to see you.”

Beau scoffs. “Her husband’s in jail because of me. I’m not winning daughter of the year anytime soon.”

She doesn’t really want to talk about it. It feels too shitty, even for her, to complain about her mom to a guy who lost his in the most god-awful way and would give anything to have her back. But her mouth keeps moving, saying, “She loves Yasha, though. Can you believe it? They have tea together. Yasha gets things from high shelves for her. It’s dis­gustingly cute.”

“This does not—huff—surprise me to hear.”

They’ve hit the western edge of the vineyard. A fence of rough-hewn petrified wood runs alongside a scattering of small geothermal pools. Little more than puddles, really—albeit puddles that stink and simmer, a brilliant coral blue at their heart and rimmed in orange.

The foothills of Mount Mentiri rear up here, dark stone protruding from the clay. Tucked into the shade of the resulting cliff is the long, low structure that houses the vats.

Some years ago, a tinkerer in Deastok came up with a clever con­traption to improve the fermentation process: iron pipes and bellows that blasted the grape must with hot air to turn it over. The fucking Stassmans adopted it at once, which Beau knows for a fact because she once snuck into their fields to see it for herself. She still remembers crouching in a bush, watching wide-eyed as the slurry of juice, skins, and tender mangled fruit-flesh swirled like an angry sea. The trapped gases of fermentation belched out in puffs of white, making the tall vats look like smokestacks.

She pitched it to her father as soon as she was back over the property line. He shot her down point-blank. And so they still churn their must the old-fashioned way here in Lionett land. Giant tubs, big wooden sticks, and workers with strong arms.

Stupid. Stupid, inflexible, risk-averse old man. Clinging tooth and nail to what he had, fearing change like the wolf at his door. All that cau­tion and control. What did it get you, Dad? An estranged daughter, a wilting wife, and iron bars.

“Just a bit farther,” she says when Caleb stoops, gasping, his hands on his knees. “C’mon. I promise the view’s worth it.”

Reprinted from Critical Role: The Mighty Nein—Children of Empire. © 2026 by Gilmore’s Glorious Goods LLC. Published by Random House Worlds, an imprint of Random House, a division of Penguin Random House LLC.

#3473. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.
