#3471. Cinematography Legend Robert Richardson Answered a Film Student’s Email — Their Conversation Became ‘The White Devil’

Robert Richardson has spent decades answering questions about how he makes movies look the way they do. The legendary cinematographer is a regular collaborator of Martin Scorsese, Oliver Stone, and Quentin Tarantino, with three Oscars to his name — for “JFK,” “The Aviator,” and “Hugo.” But something caught his attention when a film student from the Czech Republic emailed him in 2016: Jana Hojdová wanted to know about everything else.

“I get a number of requests for this kind of work and I am not really interested,” Richardson told IndieWire. “There wasn’t one that was technical. It was who are you? Where do you come from? What’s your life like?” Related Stories ‘The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan,’ Documentary About Gary Sinise’s Work with Veterans, Acquired by Freestyle Digital Media ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure

Richardson started writing Hojdová back, and a decade later, their correspondence has grown into a friendship and Hojdová’s feature directorial debut, “Robert Richardson: The White Devil.” They’ve also got an ongoing book project, which aims to organize and share even more of the film’s underlying research: an intellectual arsenal backed by the vast archives from Richardson’s house in Massachusetts.

“350 pages and we are not done,” Hojdová said, sitting next to Richardson for a Q&A after a private screening of her film at Soho House West Hollywood on October 29. “This is our homework in Los Angeles,” she said. “That we need to finish our book.” Richardson smiled.

“No is not in her vocabulary. It’s a lifetime achievement here.”

Hojdová originally approached Richardson in support of her master’s thesis at Prague’s FAMU film school. The daughter of a director and cinematographer herself, she told IndieWire she also grew up watching Richardson’s films with her family in the Czech Republic. Richardson’s first response felt “life-changing” for Hojdová and, by the time she traveled to New Zealand to meet him in 2017 on the production of Baltasar Kormákur’s “Adrift,” she said she thought she really knew the man behind the movies. In person, it became apparent just how much Hojdová still had to ask.

“I started to capture everything that he’s doing,” she said. “He’s driving [his] car to the set, his eating, everything.” Watching Richardson work and go about his daily life felt like an obvious film to Hojdová, but Richardson was less convinced. “My life is not interesting,” she recalled him saying.

Still, Hojdová kept shooting, and after six months of discussion, Richardson agreed to the project on the condition that its director would be shown, too. At first, that presented a problem for the young filmmaker who, like Richardson, greatly prefers the other side of the camera.

“I don’t like my voice, I don’t like watching myself,” she said. “It was like, ‘OK, I will say yes, but maybe I will not really be in there.’” Then, the pandemic brought her and Richardson even closer.

In 2020, what began as a short visit to look through photos and records at Richardson’s place in Cape Cod expanded as Hojdová realized just how much material the artist had kept in his basement — and lockdown forced her to extend her stay. The two ultimately wound up living together for months.

“If we didn’t have COVID, it wouldn’t be a movie,” Richardson said. “It wouldn’t be the same movie in any way at all.”

Four years after first contacting her hero, Hojdová said she knew many of Richardson’s personal stories but had previously lacked the material to put them on-screen. Suddenly, she was surrounded by countless scenes that could go with his memories, and observing Richardson, effectively in captivity, for weeks on end gave Hojdová even more to ask.

“I said to Bob that he has to be happy because we are filming at his house and he doesn’t need to go somewhere to shoot,” Hojdová said. “We are there.”

“It was really hell,” Richardson joked. “I mean seriously, you were ready to shoot every day. I had an assignment every day.” Later in the conversation, he offered another description: “She’s a spy. She convinced me that it was cool to do this, bit by bit.”

Eventually, Hojdová faced 650 hours of footage and the overwhelming task of finding the feature documentary inside it. Shaping all that material meant deciding how much of her own relationship with Richardson actually belonged on screen. It wasn’t until Hojdová reached the editing room that she fully appreciated her subject’s original condition. Viewers needed someone to accompany them into Richardson’s world — and the curious cinematographer trying to understand him? She was the way in.

“I had to fight for me being in the film, which was very hard for me because I don’t like it,” Hojdová said. “But I realized it was a great choice because I think people can connect more with me than with Bob.”

The filmmaker’s plan to bring Richardson’s personal life into conversation with the all-timer movies he helped create presented another challenge for Hojdová in post. Working extensively with executive producer Matej Chlupácek, she had to secure legal permission to use dozens of iconic images. Finishing “The White Devil” edit meant beginning an extensive licensing process, with roughly 390 entries to clear.

“It was really a nightmare, but we did it,” she said.

Of course, Richardson — whom Hojdová warmly described as “impatient” — wanted to see results as soon as possible. Still, she said he trusted the process and, more importantly, his director’s judgment.

“She was very smart,” Richardson said. “Her choices were good. She was persistent and I thought working with her was a pleasure.” Really watching the film he was asking about? That’s another matter.

Sprawled out in the front row of Soho House’s plush private theater, Richardson said the October 29 evening in L.A. felt like his first real viewing. “The White Devil” had its world premiere at the Czech Republic’s Karlovy Vary International Film Festival on July 5 and will make its North American premiere at DOC NYC on November 14. But at Karlovy Vary, where Richardson also received an award, he said he was too overwhelmed to absorb the portrait.

“I was not in body — because, then, you’re sitting in front of 1500 people and they’re playing this film,” he said. “I don’t remember half of it.”

A thrilling and sensitive consideration of cinematic genius, “The White Devil” explores Richardson’s sometimes contentious relationships with crews, his evolving collaborations with elite directors, a deeply troubled personal life, and even his experiences with psychedelic drugs. But the difficulty of living with such beautiful and raw honesty became apparent during a sweet exchange between Richardson and Hojdová in front of the Soho House audience.

Asked about watching the film, Richardson said, “When I was sitting here watching it, I was like, ‘Oh, this isn’t bad. This isn’t so bad. We could cut that down a little bit.’”

“But how was it for you to see?” Hojdová pressed in response. Richardson paused.

“I don’t like watching this movie because it’s a very transparent approach to who I am,” he said. “Most times you would think the documentary wouldn’t necessarily have as much of the shadow side.” Hojdová reminded him that exposure was part of the understanding they’d reached together: “You told me that if this film can tell someone something, it needs to be transparent.”

Speaking to the audience, Richardson turned to the subject of his five children and, as he does in “The White Devil,” took responsibility for the personal connections he sees as damaged by his deep commitment to a demanding artistic career.

“Looking back on that, it’s very hard,” he said. “I haven’t been able to fall back into a good relationship with the first two. The third has become very close.” He also reflected: “I’m trying. It’s a long time when you’re addicted to one form of drug or another. You’ve got to wean yourself off that particular methodology.”

Richardson’s youngest gave him something lighter to discuss: “I’m pretty close to the three year old, but he’s a monster,” he joked. “He is worse than I was as a child. He needs to be sent away to school now.”

Hojdová herself has a three-year-old daughter, and the adult friends’ children were born only a month apart. Still, “The White Devil” director sometimes played the parent steering Richardson onstage.

“Did you learn something?” Hojdová asked.

“I learned pain and I learned that now I should try to work harder, try to make the family work better,” Richardson said. After 10 years, a student’s shot-in-the-dark inquiry had become a genuine discovery on both sides — with each artist maturing and educating the other along the way.

“She started in her 20s in this film. Now she’s in her 30s. It’s a long time that you grow together,” Richardson said of Hojdová. “She’s seen all the worst sides of me anybody could see. She’s probably been the second longest relationship with a female in my life.”

“Robert Richardson: The White Devil” screens at DOC NYC on November 14 and 16 at IFC Center. The film is also streaming in the U.S. through November 29 with the purchase of an online screening ticket.

#3470. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3469. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3468. Pixar Promotes Jonathan Garson to President, Taking Reins from Retiring Executive Jim Morris

Jonathan Garson has been promoted to the role of president at Pixar Animation Studios, while standing executive Jim Morris moves into the role of president emeritus as he prepares for retirement. The Walt Disney Company, which owns Pixar, announced the leadership transition Wednesday afternoon.

Garson, who has notched 30 years at Disney and most recently served as Pixar’s general manager after leading its marketing and franchise team, will become president on January 4. The role will see him oversee production and operations at the animation giant, partnering with chief creative officer Pete Docter.

Disney states that Morris, who has been with Pixar for 21 years and served as president for the past 12, will remain involved with Pixar through an executive producer role on “Incredibles 3” (due out in June 2028), along with talent development, mentorship and technology initiatives. Both Garson and Morris will report to Alan Bergman, chairman of Disney Entertainment and Studios for The Walt Disney Company. Related Stories IndieWire and Disney to Celebrate Emmy Rossum and the Cast of ‘Furious’ at Special Pass the Remote Screening After ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore,’ Infinity Vision Might Turn Out to Be a Thing

“Having worked closely with Jim Morris for more than 20 years, I have enormous respect for his leadership and unwavering commitment to Pixar and its people,” Bergman wrote in a statement leading the press release on the leadership changes. “He’s not only a tremendous partner in business but a great friend. As we prepare for his eventual retirement, this transition will ensure a smooth succession for the team.”

Bergman continues, “With a deep background at both Pixar and Disney, Jonathan Garson has proven to be an exceptional leader with a strong sense of what makes Pixar unique and how its storytelling comes to life in so many ways for fans, and Pete Docter and I are excited for him to step into this role. In addition, Jonas Rivera brings a wealth of creative expertise that will serve the team well as he works even more closely with Pete.”

Morris’ statement follows: “Leading Pixar has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I’m honored to have been a steward of its legacy alongside extraordinary artists, storytellers, and technologists who keep redefining what animation can do and expanding the art of cinema. After 52 years in the business, and almost 40 at Lucasfilm and Pixar, I’ll be stepping back from the day-to-day, but I’m thrilled to move into handling a number of special projects, working alongside my friends Pete, Jonathan, and Jonas at Pixar, and of course Alan Bergman, who has been such a supporter of Pixar throughout the years. Looking ahead, I can’t think of anyone better than Jonathan to carry the legacy of this beloved studio forward. He’s a Pixar person through and through, a fierce champion of our films, our people, and our culture. Pixar is in very good hands.”

Garson then writes, “I still remember seeing ‘Toy Story’ for the first time – never imagining I’d one day work at Pixar, let alone step into a leadership role such as this. Every day I walk in the door here, I’m reminded just how special this place is and how lucky I am to be a part of it. Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support. It’s a humbling opportunity, and I look forward to working with Pete, Jonas, the production leadership team led by Katherine Sarafian and Lindsey Collins, and all of the extraordinary talent here at Pixar as we continue to push boundaries and lead our studio into the future.”

Along with Garson, Pixar will also bump Jonas Rivera to executive vice president of creative, overseeing directors, creative vice presidents, development, casting, and content advisement departments, in partnership with Docter. The two will serve as executive producers on all Pixar films.“Ever since I walked through these doors as Pixar’s first production intern, this place, its people, and its stories have been my life’s work,” said Rivera. “I am deeply honored to step into this new role alongside Pete, partnering with him and Jonathan to support our incredible filmmakers and artists. Jim has been an extraordinary mentor and leader, and I intend to build on the lessons I learned from him as we look toward our next chapter.”

Pixar is coming off of a sequel success in “Toy Story 5,” which earned over $1.1 billion at the global box office to rank as the 10th-highest-grossing animated feature of all time. Up next are two original features — “Gatto” in March and “Ghost Market” in March 2028 — followed by “Incredibles 3.”

#3467. Hit Streaming Horror Series Gets New Original Release Available Now

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "Crystal Lake"

It's often the case that exhilarating horror stories make it to the screen after having successful lives as novels—just ask Stephen King.

For Crystal Lake, though, it works the other way round. Hit Netflix horror Crystal Lake captivated viewers; a sequel to Friday the 13th, it became Peacock's fourth-biggest original scripted series in just 11 days. Even better, it's now been adapted into a new novel, courtesy of publisher A24 and horror author Tim Waggoner.

Released on October 15, Crystal Lake: The Novel follows Pamela Voohees and her rather unconventional methods of coping with her son's presumed death, to put things mildly. Of course, viewers of the original Friday the 13th will recognize Pam as the original slasher behind the hockey mask, but by the end of Crystal Lake you know what drove her to commit such heinous acts, as well as the twisted reasons she keeps committing them.

Crystal Lake gave more lore about Jason's apparent immortality, as well as plenty of character exploration for Pamela. The show demonstrates a fascinating portrayal of Pam's disturbing transformation from a concerned single mother to a suffocatingly-protective, psychologically-compromised killer. Watching her slowly fall into her psychotic spiral following Jason's supposed drowning, as well as her vice-like attachment to Grace as a perversion of the mother-child dynamic, are already a captivating watch. The novel will surely gave an even better look into Pam's interior life, and the adaptation could be even more valuable too..

For those who don't want to lose the slasher elements of this franchise, don't fret: Crystal Lake The Novel doesn't seem as though it'll shy away from some of the grisly kill scenes seen in the show. After all, the novel's author is the pen behind the official Terrifier novel tie-ins. But beyond the violence enacted by Pamela (and Jason and Grace), the novelization could shine a brighter light on some of the arguably more disturbing of the series.

Crystal Lake features cold-hearted medical abuse, notably in flashback scenes of Pam's pregnancy and Jason's early childhood. The show reveals that Project Argonaut, the immoral medical experiment orchestrated by Bellflower, is responsible for Jason's ability to heal quickly from injuries and to grow stronger and larger in so short a time. Episode nine already shows the fate of the experiment's conductor at the hands of Pamela, but the novel could give us so much more detail on the project itself. These flashback scenes could show us Pam's turmoil during and shortly following pregnancy, allowing for some truly disturbing body horror-adjacent writing.

Given this is the case, Crystal Lake viewers who loved the expanding lore and characters will surely be drawn to this novelization. Running at 448 pages, it has room to be a classic slasher as well as a deep dive into Pam's twisted mind.

The novel is available now on A24's official site, with expanded buying options inevitably coming soon.

#3466. 10 Best Stephen King Books of All Time, Ranked According to Goodreads

Stephen King is the undisputed master of literary horror. No one else in the genre comes close to him in terms of quality or quality. He has penned over 60 novels and 200 short stories, continuously captivating readers with his exploration of the dark corners of the human psyche. His best works, like The Shining, It, and Misery, are not just tales of terror but profound examinations of family, addiction, and madness. In addition, they are great snapshots of late 20th-century America, particularly its small towns.

Indeed, King's talents go beyond horror, as evidenced in more dramatic stories like The Shawshank Redemption and The Green Mile. His writing is also highly visual, lending itself well to the screen. Some of the greatest movies of all time have been made based on his work. This dense, varied bibliography means he's sure to continue frightening readers for generations to come. Those looking to get started with his work could do worse than to look to his most highly-rated books on the review site Goodreads. These are King's best projects, ranked according to its users.

"And then the world exploded." King's electric debut revolves around a shy, bullied high school girl with a deeply religious and abusive mother. Her life takes a drastic turn when she discovers her telekinetic powers. After being humiliated at her prom by a cruel prank, Carrie unleashes her newfound abilities in a fit of rage, leading to a night of devastation in her small town.

The book is short (not even 200 pages) but packs an outsize punch. It's also structurally inventive, including excerpts from fictional books, newspapers, and reports, as well as contributions from various narrators. Reportedly, King grew dissatisfied with the book early on in the writing process, discarding the pages he'd written in the trash. His wife Tabitha retrieved them and insisted he continue. It's a good thing she did: Carrie was a bestseller, launching its author's career and helping to bring horror fiction into the mainstream.

"Death is a mystery, and burial is a secret." Louis Creed moves with his family to a rural town in Maine, where he discovers a nearby pet cemetery with a dark secret. When tragedy strikes and Louis's son, Gage, is killed in an accident, he learns of an ancient burial ground beyond the pet cemetery that can bring the dead back to life, but at a terrible cost. Pet Sematary features some of the oldest horror tropes around, like a character who violates the finality of death and must suffer the consequences.

However, King breathes new life into these old chestnuts and makes them chilling once more. In large part, this is because the characters are complex and believable. They feel like real people, and the reader sympathizes with them, making their ordeals all the more horrific. For these reasons, Guillermo del Toro has said it's one of the books he would most like to adapt. "As a father, I now understand it better than I ever would have, and it scares me a hundred times more," he explains.

"When the evil falls on the town, its coming seems almost preordained." 'Salem's Lot centers on Ben Mears, a writer who returns to his hometown to find inspiration for his new book. However, he soon discovers that the townspeople are falling prey to a sinister force — a centuries-old vampire named Kurt Barlow. Once again, King takes a well-worn idea — in this case, a vampire story — but reinvigorates it by relocating the action to a fresh setting: a small New England town in the mid-70s.

King has described the book as "Peyton Place meets Dracula", which is accurate. In a lesser writer's hands, this tale might have come out fangless, but 'Salem's Lot is decidedly creepy and compelling. In addition to the vampire thrills, the small-town drama is intriguing as well. The book is populated with a large cast of realistic characters, all of whom have their own struggles and secrets. This recipe translated well to the screen, resulting in a terrific miniseries adaptation. A new film version is in development as well.

"I am your number one fan." King gets a little meta with this psychological thriller in which a bestselling author, Paul Sheldon, is kidnapped by his "number one fan," Annie Wilkes, after a car accident. Annie, a former nurse with a dangerous fixation on Paul's work, forces him to write a new novel that revives her favorite character, Misery Chastain. Trapped in Annie's remote home, Paul endures physical and psychological torture as he struggles to escape her clutches.

The book is incredibly tense. The reader roots desperately for Paul to break free, only to have their hopes dashed repeatedly. King's protagonists are often authors (write what you know, and all that), but Paul might be his most vivid and likable. He's definitely a little autobiographical, too. King has said that Paul feeling chained to his Misery character was a stand-in for King feeling boxed into the horror genre. He has also said that Annie Wilkes is a metaphor for drug addiction.

"Terrible things happen in the world, and they're things no one can explain." Struggling writer and recovering alcoholic Jack Torrance takes a job as the winter caretaker of the Overlook Hotel, a remote resort with a sinister history. He brings with him his wife, Wendy, and their young son, Danny, who possesses psychic abilities. As winter sets in, the hotel's malevolent influence begins to fray Jack's sanity.

Though not quite as good as Stanley Kubrick's film version, The Shining is top-tier King, and certainly one of his scariest books. It was his third published novel and is considerably more ambitious than Carrie and 'Salem's Lot, which had preceded it. Here, he draws inspiration from Edgar Allan Poe and Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House but filters it through his distinctive perspective. The result is an intelligent ghost story that elevates character over gore or action.

"Books are a uniquely portable magic." On Writing is a hybrid book: part memoir, part guidebook for aspiring writers. Here, King shares his journey from a struggling writer to a bestselling author, providing insights into his creative process, work ethic, and the experiences that shaped his stories. It's chock-full of simple but powerful writing advice, placing it among the best works on the topic. King's description of his work habits is especially fascinating.

King wrote the book while recovering from being hit by a van, and his inner struggles are evident on the page. This was clearly a difficult project for him. However, the book is also impressive and triumphant, with King rediscovering his voice, creativity, and passion for the craft. As a result, On Writing is a moving book that can be appreciated by anyone, not just budding writers or horror fans. It's one of the strongest works the author has ever produced.

"Because the dark surrounds us, let us turn our faces to the light." 11/22/63 is a uniquely King blend of historical fiction and time travel. The novel follows Jake Epping, a high school teacher who discovers a portal to the year 1958 in the back of a diner. He sets out on a mission to prevent JFK's assassination on November 22, 1963. Soon, Epping bonds with people from the past, finding himself torn between times.

The premise is a little ridiculous, but King pulls it off, resulting in one of his most sweeping, moving novels. His recreation of the '50s and '60s is immersive, reflecting the huge amount of research he did while writing it. The characters are also well-drawn, particularly Jake's fiancée Sadie. This means that when tragedy strikes, it hits the reader even harder. Perhaps as a result, 11/22/63 was one of King's most acclaimed novels of the 2010s, with the New York Times going so far as to rank it among the top five fiction books of the year.

"We lie best when we lie to ourselves." It is a monumental work of horror that delves into the nature of fear and the power of memory. It alternates between two timelines, following a group of friends known as the Losers' Club as children in the 1950s and as adults in the 1980s. The friends are united by their encounters with a malevolent entity that takes the form of their worst fears, most often appearing as a clown named Pennywise.

King wasn't the first writer to describe a monster that takes on the form of whatever its victim fears most, but he certainly did it the most memorably. Pennywise is now an iconic villain, in his literary and cinematic forms: the shot of him peeking out from a sewer is seared into many people's brains. Beneath the frights, though, It is a smart, frustrating, overlong, controversial but undeniably imaginative work and a standout of '80s horror.

"That wasn't any act of God." Another King epic, The Stand takes place in the aftermath of a global pandemic that has wiped out most of the human population. The survivors are drawn into two factions: one led by the kind and wise Mother Abagail, and the other by the sinister and charismatic Randall Flagg. As the survivors rebuild their lives, they must prepare for an inevitable confrontation between the forces of good and evil.

This is essentially King's take on Lord of the Rings but set in a post-apocalyptic version of Las Vegas. It features bomb blasts, supernatural powers, countless characters, and the vilest of villains. Although not one of his most accessible books for newcomers, The Stand is vivid, intense, and grand in scale. The extended edition clocks in at well over 1000 pages. It's probably the most ambitious thing King has ever done. Critics responded; both Time magazine and the BBC have ranked The Stand among the best books of all time.

"Sometimes there is absolutely no difference at all between salvation and damnation." King's highest-rated book on Goodreads is less of a horror and more of a supernatural drama. The Green Mile takes place in the 1930s at Cold Mountain Penitentiary's death row. The story is narrated by Paul Edgecombe, a former prison guard who recounts his experiences with John Coffey, a giant of a man convicted of murdering two young girls. Despite his imposing appearance, Coffey possesses an extraordinary gift: the ability to heal others and absorb their suffering.

The death row setting is unique and memorable, and it's a great vehicle for King to explore issues of morality and justice. The Green Mile covers a lot of ground, pivoting from sweet and poignant to violent and horrifying. Like King's story Rita Hayworth and Shawshank Redemption, it was adapted into an excellent film by director Frank Darabont. It's a great example of King's range and thoughtful handling of incendiary subject matter.

#3464. ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

Early in “Black Doves” Season 2, Helen (Keira Knightley) experiences a beautiful, partial epiphany. She and her best friend Sam (Ben Whishaw) have been busy, once again, keeping each other alive. She’s trying to find her missing handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire). He’s working through a list of increasingly challenging assassinations, urged on by an unknown and unwelcome new boss.

But then Helen realizes, “We’re looking for the same answers. We thought we were in separate shit creeks, but actually we’re in the same shit creek, paddling together.”

Sam, never one to let a misapplied analogy slide (nor one to avoid noting the glass is also half empty), quickly informs her what she’s suggesting doesn’t make sense. “There is no paddle,” he says. “That’s the whole second half of the saying: ‘up shit creek without a paddle.'” Related Stories Watch ‘The Greatest’ Team Discuss How They Made the Impossible ‘Possible’ on Muhammad Ali Series ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart

So the two spies may be in the same boat, on the same river, in the same circumstance — whatever — but they’re still stuck there, paddle-less, likely to drown in particularly unpleasant fashion.

Except the two of them being in the same creek isn’t Helen’s epiphany. This is: “I think friendship is the paddle,” Helen says.

And she’s right. Of course she’s right. It’s a treacly sentiment, but it’s still a beautiful one: love guiding you through a life that seems hopeless. In fact, she’s more right than she realizes, which is why it’s only a partial epiphany — she and Sam will recognize the rest as “Black Doves” works its way through another excellent season of existential espionage action.

If you don’t remember everything from the first six episodes of Joe Barton’s series, don’t worry. Catching up is easy and enjoyable if you have the time for a rewatch, and even if you don’t, Season 2 is more of an expansion on previous scenes with a fresh set of antagonists, allies, and agonized choices for our dear spies, wading their way through an identity crisis.

Helen herself says there’s been “a lot of big changes” during her couples’ therapy session with her husband, Wallace (Andrew Buchan), referencing not only his ascension to Prime Minister but her subsequent sink to subservience. Turns out it’s hard to be a secret agent when you’re married to the most prominent politician in the United Kingdom. Sure, she gets to live on Downing Street and meet the queen, but passing state secrets isn’t as stimulating when all you have to do to get them is suffer through dinner after dinner with various delegates.

What’s really eating at Helen, though, is what being a “spy wife” implies: disempowerment. She’s essentially a go-between, ratting on her husband to her own higher-ups, so when Reed suddenly disappears and she’s asked to report to a bunch of suits she’s never even seen before, it further activates her nagging lack of agency. “I would like to know who the hell it is I’m risking my life, liberty, and fucking freedom for,” Helen snaps at her nameless bosses, led by Mr. Conteh (“Alien: Earth” breakout Babou Ceesay).

Wouldn’t we all? As it did in its first season, “Black Doves” excels at making its shoot-em-up spy series relatable (while winking here and there at the genre itself). Helen’s feelings of disenfranchisement reflect the growing divide between the working and executive classes; between the people who are told what to do (at the risk of losing our paychecks, healthcare, and everything each of them protects) and the ones doing the telling (who risk less and less, as they move further into the belly of the beast). The slick series keeps these parallels on the subtle side, never allowing its messaging to interfere with its drama, action, or humor. But it’s there, and it draws us to these characters via a kind of intrinsic veracity.

Helen wants to understand what’s being done with the information she provides. She wants to be rewarded for her immense efforts, not in money, but with a seat at the table. Last season, she nearly left the spy trade altogether to run away with a man who turned out to be conning her. (He was a spy, too.) Now, she’s not only doubling down on her commitment to her job, but also her family — she loves Wallace and wants to make it work, hence the couples therapy.

Her discontent is shared by Sam, who’s in his own powerless predicament. After getting busted by the cops following a successful hit, he’s approached by a “private entity” that offers to make the homicide charges disappear in exchange for completing four assassinations of their choosing. He takes the deal (the devil you know, and all that), but soon discovers what makes his assignments “difficult” aren’t just the armed guards surrounding each target; it’s the identities of each target paired with not knowing why they’ve been chosen to die.

“Love is a weakness,” the private entity’s representative tells Sam. “And you’re full of it.” Huh, where have I heard that line of thinking before? “Black Doves” is well-timed, arriving two days after America’s full-throated rejection of MAGA’s misguided moralism, and it does a fine job illustrating why anyone trying to manipulate our feelings for their own gains is not to be trusted; why compassion for our fellow man is what saves us, rather than what holds us down.

Granted, it can be a little hard to believe Sam would buy into such a plainly vile argument, but Season 2 puts him in such a despondent state, it’s easier to accept his being led astray. His cycle of heavy drinking and little sleep also allows Whishaw to convincingly shade his character in a shifting desperation that turns on a dime. One moment, he’s angry, the next he’s depressed, and the next he’s can’t keep a dark joke from slipping out. Throughout, there’s a lingering sadness, which is properly explored in a superb episode made up of a trifecta of flashbacks, and his dour constitution still pairs perfectly with Helen’s reassuring nature. He saves her time and time again, just by answering her call, and she saves him, time and time again, by seeing him even when he can’t see himself.

Joining the party — and Season 2 is a party, peppered with sharp jokes, punctuated by smart needle drops, and paced at a steady, compulsive tempo — are Laila (Ambika Mod), the self-described “muscle” assigned to help Helen on a messy mission; Cecile (Neve Campbell), the U.S. Defense Envoy tasked with telling the Prime Minister what to do (not that he listens); Reed, who gets a stronger arc better suited for Lancashire’s deft command; and Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy), two energetic young hitmen-for-hire who are coming to learn that love and happiness aren’t guaranteed outcomes, especially for people whose lives are regularly at risk.

“We’re all just animals, aren’t we?,” Williams says in a drug-induced moment of reflection. “Living with the things that we’ve done, living with the consequences of our actions. Looking for purpose, for connection, for love. And maybe we’ll never find it.”

Or maybe you will. Maybe you just better consider who’s standing next to you when the bullets start flying, figuratively or literally. Maybe you just need to see who still sees you when you’re beaten down by the powers that be. Maybe you just have to realize we’re all up a creek at some point, and the only paddle you really need is a friend who’s willing to wade through the shit — or pull you out of it.

“Black Doves” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

From construction moratoriums on data centers to lawsuits, Musk is facing new challenges

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars trying to help Republicans win the 2026 midterm elections. Instead, Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, Texas elected a Democratic governor for the first time in more than three decades, and voters across the country backed new restrictions on AI data centers.

For Musk, those election results might have consequences beyond Washington since the billionaire has invested heavily in the infrastructure needed to power AI. Musk has massive data centers that support his Grok chatbot and agent Grok Bot and has built a significant part of his business empire in Texas. The incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, making her election particularly relevant to Musk's AI infrastructure expansion in Texas.

Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️November 4, 2026

According to campaign finance reporting from The New York Times, Musk contributed approximately $474 million to political groups and candidates during the 2026 election cycle.

The money included roughly $216 million for his America PAC and $168 million for the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed Republican Senate candidates.

Musk appeared to acknowledge the losses early Wednesday morning, joking on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time."

Jokes aside, Hinojosa's win is significant since Musk has relocated major business operations to Texas, and SpaceX has plans to expand its computing infrastructure at its Starbase complex in Boca Chica.

According to Reuters, chip research firm SemiAnalysis has identified more than 9 gigawatts of planned or developing computing capacity associated with Musk's AI ambitions, including projects in Texas.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

But companies planning new facilities may face longer approval processes, closer scrutiny of their electricity consumption and changes to the financial incentives that made Texas attractive in the first place.

Musk's political losses coincided with a broader change in public attitudes toward data centers. According to The Verge's November 4 election analysis, 45 local ballot measures addressed data center development nationwide. By Wednesday morning, results from 33 favored restrictions on construction.

Those restrictions varied considerably. Some communities supported temporary construction moratoriums, while others voted to prohibit facilities above certain electricity-demand thresholds.

In El Dorado, Kansas, voters approved a 10-year ban on data centers with peak electrical demand exceeding 10 megawatts. In Wells, Maine, voters favored a temporary moratorium on large facilities.

The concerns driving these votes have become familiar to residents living near proposed data centers: electricity prices, water consumption, noise, pollution and the question of who should pay for expensive infrastructure upgrades.

An NBC News Election Day poll also found that 76% of respondents opposed having a data center in their community.

The political shift aside, Musk's AI infrastructure was already facing challenges. Near Memphis, Tennessee, his company's Colossus data centers rely on enormous amounts of computing power to train and operate AI models.

The operation has also generated complaints from surrounding communities about the natural gas turbines used to provide electricity.

On October 30, a federal judge rejected a motion to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the NAACP over turbines operating in Southaven, Mississippi.

The lawsuit alleges that the turbines require air permits and expose nearby residents to harmful pollution.

These disputes are separate from Tuesday's election results, but they illustrate the regulatory and community opposition that can complicate even projects already under development.

Musk's companies have already committed substantial resources to computing infrastructure, and demand for AI processing capacity continues to drive expansion across the industry.

But now Texas could introduce new restrictions on development and local communities now have more political support for proposed facilities. For consumers, we might see more protections against higher electricity bills, increased water consumption and pollution near data centers. But, none of those changes will happen overnight.

America's data center boom isn't ending, but the companies building the infrastructure behind AI may have a harder time expanding.

#3461. ‘Tender Loving Care’ Trailer: Mike Leigh’s Likely Final Film Pairs Him with a Career-Best Kate O’Flynn

Kate O’Flynn is the belle of the ball in 2026 after winning an Emmy for Apple TV’s “Twin Peaks”-esque small-town mystery series “Widow’s Bay.” But even those fans of her socially clumsy and feverishly party-planning mayor’s assistant Patricia on that series may not be prepared for her soulful, wrenching work in Mike Leigh’s latest film. “Tender Loving Care,” opening in select theaters December 11, may also be the 83-year-old director’s last one due to age. Watch the trailer below.

In this latest film from the British director of “Secrets and Lies,” “Vera Drake,” “Naked,” and “Hard Truths” — all movies where, like this one, he starts without a script and works instead on building the story and characters with his actors — O’Flynn is joined by Alice Bailey Johnson, Marion Bailey, and Paul Jesson. O’Flynn plays government child protection worker Amy, reeling from a breakup, who moves back in with her best friend from childhood, the upbeat social worker Rosie (Bailey Johnson). Amy’s parents (Bailey and Jesson) are meanwhile dealing with aging, which leads to a heartbreaking final crisis. Related Stories Cinematography Legend Robert Richardson Answered a Film Student’s Email — Their Conversation Became ‘The White Devil’ ‘The Ballad of Lieutenant Dan,’ Documentary About Gary Sinise’s Work with Veterans, Acquired by Freestyle Digital Media

“Tender Loving Care” played Telluride, Toronto International Film Festival, San Sebastian, New York Film Festival, London Film Festival, and more, all to strong response. Bleecker Street will open the movie in New York and Los Angeles on December 11, followed by an expansion beginning December 25. Most recently, “Tender Loving Care” received four Gotham Award nominations, including International Feature, Director, Original Screenplay, and Outstanding Supporting Performance (O’Flynn). O’Flynn previously had very small roles in Leigh films including “Happy-Go-Lucky,” “Mr. Turner,” and “Peterloo.”

From IndieWire’s review: “Said to be Mike Leigh’s final film, the simple but profoundly affecting ‘Tender Loving Care‘ confronts the dominant theme of his career — the practice and value of communal support in the face of an unforgiving world — with the directness of a closing statement. Here, in an exquisitely rendered microportrait about a week in the lives of two sparkling London social workers, Leigh gets right to the heart of the matter. The result is one of his most formidable stories in spite of its scope; spartan and straightforward, absent plot complication but awash in pointillistic detail, this so-called swan song collects its attention into a bracingly humane look at conflicting networks of care. It exalts in what love and tenderness can do for a person, and just as honestly pays heed to what they can’t.”

You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3459. ABC Pays Off Gregory’s Oldest Abbott Elementary Promise Right On Time

While it might have been over five years since Abbott Elementary first introduced Gregory and Jacob to each other, the ABC sitcom still paid off the pair’s relationship promise at the perfect time in season 6, episode 4, “Halloween Party.” Abbott Elementary’s entire cast of characters are iconic, even if the inimitable custodian Mr. Johnson remains the sitcom’s standout for this writer’s money.

Even if Mr. Johnson’s best Abbott Elementary moments are highlights of the iconic workplace sitcom, the show works as a whole because its cast has such strong chemistry with each other. Of course, Janine and Gregory’s Abbott Elementary love story provides a core for the narrative evolution of the show, but like Jim and Pam in The Office or Amy and Jake in Brooklyn Nine-Nine, the pair's romance is only part of the larger appeal of the ensemble series.

The complicated, ever-changing relationship between Janine and Principal Ava, or the heroine’s nuanced relationship with her professional mentor and surrogate mother Barb, are just as important to Quinta Brunson’s cheery schoolteacher as her romance with Gregory. Similarly, Gregory’s own relationships with his co-workers have led him to grow and change over the years, too. In season 6, episode 4, “Halloween Party,” the delayed payoff to one Abbott Elementary gag proved just how much the character has transformed.

Ever since Janine and Gregory got together at the end of season 3, Abbott Elementary’s iconic couple have pulled out all the stops when it comes to their couple’s costumes for Halloween. Whether they went as Jurassic Park’s Mr. DNA and a DNA strand in season 4, episode 4, “Costume Contest,” or Sinners director Ryan Coogler and an IMAX screen in season 5, episode 5, “Camping,” the duo always had a plan that, at the very least, seemed to make sense to them.

Thus, it was a shock when “Halloween Party” saw Gregory dress as Hey Arnold’s supporting star Gerald Johanssen, while Janine dressed as Rugrats supporting character Susie Carmichael. Of course, Abbott Elementary season 6’s Halloween costumes soon made sense when Jacob explained to the show’s in-universe camera crew that he asked Gregory to do a couple’s Halloween costume with him the first day they met.

Assuming he would only be working as a substitute teacher at the eponymous school for a few weeks or months while he waited for a principal role to open up elsewhere, Gregory blithely replied that he would gladly be the Gerald to Jacob’s Arnold, ‘in five years.’ Five years later, “Halloween Party” paid off this setup as, while he might have rolled his eyes about it, Gregory not only went through with the costume, but even admitted that he liked the fit.

This isn't the first time that a sitcom has set up a punchline a long time in advance, as evidenced by The Simpsons paying off a gag about Moe over a year after another unrelated episode set up the joke. However, the costume joke does draw some welcome attention to Abbott Elementary’s most overlooked pairing, Jacob and Gregory. As far back as season 1, episode 5, “Student Transfer,” Jacob has always been eager to ingratiate himself with his co-worker.

However, in typical Abbott Elementary fashion, the acclaimed sitcom isn’t content to keep this dynamic static over the years lest it run the risk of feeling tired. By season 2, episode 11, “Read-A-Thon,” Jacob and Gregory were already on more equal terms when the duo ran a podcast club together with the school’s older students.

By season 2, episode 14, “Valentine’s Day,” Jacob had gotten so close with Gregory that he was among the first to notice his crush on Janine. In season 3, episode 11, “Double Date,” the pair’s original dynamic was flipped completely as Abbott Elementary’s Gregory was the one to embarrass Jacob with his ridiculous spying on Janine during the titular double date.

Giovana Gelhoren is a High-Trending Topics Writer at Collider, covering the most-talked-about stars, movies, and TV shows. Before joining Collider, she was a Digital News Writer at People Magazine and served as Associate Editor at SheKnows, where she honed her expertise in celebrity coverage and entertainment journalism.

A proud Latina from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Giovana graduated from Northwestern University with a degree in Journalism and International Studies. She has interviewed countless celebrities, including Anne Hathaway, Halle Berry, Pamela Anderson, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Brenda Song, and is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of film, TV, and pop culture.

When it comes to network TV, ABC has been dominating with consistent, chart-topping shows for many years now. Between High Potential, starring It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia's Kaitlin Olson as the hyper-intelligent single mother Morgan Gillory, and the newcomer R.J. Decker, led by Scott Speedman as an ex-con photographer turned P.I., the network has found critical acclaim and strong viewership alike.

But while High Potential and R.J. Decker are certainly a few of the latest successes from the network, Will Trent, which was first released in January 2023, has also been going strong since its release. With Season 5 of the series already confirmed, the crime series has proven to have a killer procedural formula, one that draws in viewers with episodic cases while still developing major storylines for the main characters. And while it might not be getting the same attention as other ABC shows right now, it's the perfect binge for crime fans and ABC shows alike.

Will Trent, based on Karin Slaughter's bestselling series of crime novels, follows the titular special agent (Ramón Rodríguez) at the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. Abandoned at birth and growing up in the harsh environment of Atlanta's overburdened foster care system, Trent parlayed his experience into a unique perspective on crime that has helped him post a remarkable clearance rate and become renowned for his dedication. Along the way, he's still had to wrestle with his past and other personal challenges in the pursuit of justice.

Throughout its run, Will Trent has seen massive, and growing, success. Season 4 was the most-viewed installment of Will Trent to date, becoming the first series on the network since Scandal to grow in ratings every single year it's been on the air. In fact, it's the first broadcast show across all networks to accomplish the feat in nearly 14 years, according to Nielsen's measure. On Rotten Tomatoes, the series also received critical acclaim, reaching an impressive 89% from critics in Season 1. While the following seasons have yet to earn a critics score, reviews say it all. "Will Trent continues to go deeper into its characters’ lives and psyches, transforming the show from an average crime procedural to one of the best character-driven dramas on any broadcast network," writes one critic review from Season 4, which premiered on January 6, 2026.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Season 5 of Will Trent, which will be premiering on January 6, 2027, already revealed some major plans for the new season. Among them is the addition of The Pitt actress Alexandra Metz, who has been tapped to play Birdie Palmer, the newly appointed Deputy Director of the GBI. Reports say that Birdie is confident and ambitious, but she is "deeply guarded after a traumatic event in her past."

The Ramón Rodríguez-led series just got a major update.

Metz's arrival comes at a pivotal point after the unexpected and controversial death of Amanda (Sonja Sohn) in the Season 4 finale. Speaking with Variety, showrunner Karine Rosenthal explained why Amanda’s death creates such a major reset for the show. “Amanda has been the character who has protected Will for as long as she has known him. So this gives us the opportunity for a completely new dynamic in the GBI, because her replacement will not have that same relationship with Will," she said. "Her death had the most impact on the most amount of characters. It really sets everybody reeling from this enormous loss. So it’s such a reset for our characters in a way that is painful but exciting for Season 5.”

With all that said, while that cliffhanger from Season 4 had some fans reeling, the fans' dedication to the show continues to prove how much of a hit Will Trent is on ABC. With a hardened yet endearing lead who audiences can't help but to root for, and episodic cases that keep viewers guessing, the series is another home run for ABC, as well as an easy, satisfying binge for anyone who hasn't been tuning in.

Special Agent Will Trent was abandoned at birth and endured a harsh coming-of-age in Atlanta's overwhelmed foster care system. Determined to make sure no one feels as he did, he now has the highest clearance rate.

#3456. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

Geoffrey Hinton gives his latest thoughts on the evolving tech

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Geoffrey Hinton’s name has been making the rounds a lot more often nowadays due to his commentary on the very technology his research helped develop.

During an interview with the Financial Times, he predicted who will benefit financially the most from the continued evolution of AI. “It's going to create massive unemployment and a huge rise in profits,” he pointed out. “It will make a few people much richer and most people poorer. That's not AI's fault, that is the capitalist system.”

And during an appearance on The Diary Of A CEO podcast, Hinton gave his thoughts on the topic of AI being misused and the associated risks that come with it. “There's risks that come from people misusing AI, and that's most of the risks and all of the short-term risks,” he noted. “And then there's risks that come from AI getting super smart and understanding it doesn't need us.”

Now he’s back in the news for (once again) giving a stern warning about AI. Here’s what he had to say during his latest interview.

During a conversation with The Guardian, Hinton made it clear that he doesn’t see himself as an AI doomer and that he genuinely believes that AI has the potential to lead to great things happening in the future. But he balanced out that optimistic outlook with a more sobering one when he stated that “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it.”

Hinton also gave a very blunt answer when the discussion moved over to the major leaders backing the companies that keep releasing even more advanced versions of their signature models. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a s**t,” he said. “They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.” As Hinton’s conversation with The Guardian continued, he presented the idea of a federal agency that keeps a close eye on AI and makes sure the companies that develop it release it in the safest state possible.

“We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released,” he declared. “We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

One of Hinton’s other more recent comments about AI that proved to be alarming for many was said during a CNN segment. Simply put, he warned everyone that the threat of humanity’s destruction via AI is a real possibility if we don’t get it under control. “If we don’t figure out how to make it safe, there’s a real possibility it could destroy us,” he declared. “We’ve never made things that are smarter than ourselves. We don’t know what it’s like to deal with them.” He went on to say that it would simply be “foolish to keep developing these things until we understand how we can live with them.”

Hinton’s sentiments about AI fall in line with most of the American voters who made their voices heard against the technology. According to Data Centers on the Ballot, 37 measures aimed at restricting data center development have won over a single measure that’s attached to allowing the continued expansion of those same centers.

And while the Trump administration’s push for AI and renaming it “Super Intelligence” has made the rounds, Americans are largely pushing back against those initiatives (as evidenced by this site’s current 90.5% rate of people who oppose data centers). Even with Hinton’s negative sentiments about AI while speaking with The Guardian, he remained optimistic about humanity and the ability to intervene to keep it under control.

“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he proclaimed. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”

#3454. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.
