Knightley and Ben Whishaw return with razor-sharp banter, tangled conspiracies and plenty of bloodshed

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Black Doves" was one of my favorite surprises of 2024. A spy thriller with a panache for murder, double-crosses and dark comedy? Netflix, you really do know me.

Verdict: "Black Doves" season 2 is a thoroughly entertaining return, with plenty of twists, sharp humor and terrific performances from Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw. It occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets, but the show's winning mix of spy games and genuine friendship makes this another binge-worthy winner.

Release schedule: All 6 episodes now streaming

Now, Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw are back for another round as secret agent Helen Webb and her hitman best friend, Sam Young. I've watched all six episodes of "Black Doves" season 2, and I'm happy to report that creator Joe Barton has done it again. This is a terrific installment, with plenty of twists, sharp dialogue and wonderfully messy characters.

So what makes this return such a success? Well, there are a few things, starting with deeper insights into the backgrounds of several major players.

Kelly most recently reviewed "The Gilded Age" season 4, "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

Helen is still feeding government secrets to the Black Doves, the shadowy organization that employs her, while her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) is about to become prime minister. You'd think that would be enough to keep her occupied, but there's another crisis brewing. Her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), is accused of plotting a coup against the organization, putting Helen and Sam in the middle of yet another sticky situation.

It leads to some fascinating revelations about Mrs. Reed's past, including a family connection that turns out to be rather more complicated (and deadly) than anyone expected. I particularly enjoyed the flashbacks to her earlier life; getting a better sense of how Reed became the woman she is today makes her even more interesting. It also gives the world of "Black Doves" a richer history and texture.

The plotting does get pretty convoluted at times. There are a lot of people with competing agendas, and keeping track of who's working for whom and whose loyalties lie where can feel like a full-time job. But honestly, that's part of the appeal. Just when you think you've figured out what's going on, someone turns out to be working for someone else, usually with a gun on hand. It's all very entertaining.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The returning cast is in fine form, particularly Knightley and Whishaw, whose chemistry remains one of the best things about the show. Helen and Sam's friendship is the heart of "Black Doves." You can see their genuine affection for each other, even when they're busy shooting at various foes. Sam has his own demons to contend with this season, and as compelling as that storyline is, the show is strongest when the two of them are in a scene together.

Season 2 also brings in some welcome new faces, most notably Ambika Mod as Laila, an acerbic Black Doves agent who helps Helen with a heist (while toting a big gun, of course). Mod is fantastic, bringing a wonderfully snarky energy to the proceedings and delivering some of the season's best lines.

Not everyone makes quite the same impression. Neve Campbell joins as American envoy Cecile Mason, but her character doesn't get much to do. It's a bit of a waste of an actor and I'm still scratching my head about why someone of Campbell's caliber was cast in such a nothingburger of a role.

There's a lot of competition in the spy thriller department these days, but "Black Doves" continues to hold its own. It's got the action and intrigue you'd expect from the genre, but it also has a sense of humor that keeps things from getting too serious.

Season 2 isn't without its shortcomings. A few characters could use more screen time, and the plot occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets. But those are relatively minor complaints when you've got the kind of cracking cast that could make a dictionary recital work.

Most of all, I'm just glad we get another six episodes with Helen and Sam. Their friendship gives the show something beyond the usual spy-versus-spy shenanigans. If you enjoyed season 1, season 2 is just as good. And there's plenty of story left for "Black Doves" to continue for at least one more outing, but I hope it's more like three or four.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3376. Here’s everything new Apple TV has coming in November

Apple TV’s November lineup includes the return of a beloved comedy, a heist thriller with big stars, the follow-up film to its Oscar winner, and a lot more. Here’s everything new coming to Apple TV in November.

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery.

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

In the latest special under the acclaimed “Snoopy Presents” banner, the Peanuts kids are on their best behavior — but Snoopy has landed on Santa’s naughty list. With just 12 days until Christmas, he sets out to prove he’s not such a bad beagle after all, discovering along the way that the season is about more than gifts.

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

#3375. Jordan Firstman Knows When It’s Time to Leave the Party

Even hard-partying clubgoers worth their weight in white-label records run the risk of staying at the party too long. Thankfully, Jordan Firstman has figured out, through years of trial and error, the perfect time to call it a night.

“It’s 4am,” Firstman says, during a visit to the Rolling Stone Studio. “If you’re really partying, 4am is perfect. It’s before the sun comes up, and then you can be up and still go to the gym.”

The writer, director, and star of Club Kid knows of what he speaks. A longtime fixture in New York City nightlife and a regular at hot spots like Basement, Firstman had been spending a lot of time in Berlin doing what he termed an “excessive” amount of party drugs (“a lot of different letters, a lot of different numbers”) when he realized he needed to slow things down. Then, at a dinner party, he began talking a friend’s kid and “I was saying a bunch of inappropriate stuff around [him]. Everyone was laughing. I thought, ‘Oh, there’s something here.'”

Those two factors helped inspire Firstman’s directorial debut, a story of a club promoter named Peter who ends up having a particularly wild night out. Ten years later, someone shows up at his door and introduces him to the son (played by newcomer Reggie Absalom) he never knew he had. The reluctant dad and his kid end up bonding, as fatherhood inspires this thirtysomething to grow up and leave his drugging days behind him. “It’s like Kramer vs. Ketamine,” Firstman says, namechecking the 1979 Oscar-winner.

A massive hit at Cannes — where Firstman and his cast and crew ended up on a yacht during the premiere’s after–after-party and admittedly did not adhere to the 4am rule — the movie ended up being picked up by A24 and is now one of the buzzier movies schlepping its way through awards season. For Firstman, however, seeing his cast, many of whom he pulled directly from the LGBTQ+ clubgoing community, was already a dream come true. “We made this story that is filled with with real queer people from the community, and these amazing trans women, Firstman says, tearing up. “So for me, the most moving part was seeing them on the red carpet — all of a sudden everyone’s hair is blowing like Beyonce, and they start playing Whitney Houston… and it’s the most magical moment ever. Seeing queer people be able to shine like that, on that stage in front of the whole world. It was just like, we don’t get these opportunities much. It was just really cool to see.”

Also in the interview, Firstman talked about why his role in I Love L.A. reflects his own ambitiousness, another actress he’d write a song about after having penned that famous ode to Laura Dern, and what he and Whitney Houston have in common. #3374. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

Apple’s current MacBook Pro lineup features multiple different tiers:

#3372. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3371. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

What do you think of this multitasking change in iPadOS 27.2? Do you think Apple should apply its iPhone Duo learnings to the iPad? Let us know in the comments.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 combines outstanding smart features with solid sports tracking to be one of the best all-round options on the market.

The Pace 4 Pro is a thin, lightweight sports watch with a bright AMOELD display and impressive battery life.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro and Apple Watch Ultra 4 both launched in September this year and both impressed me in my testing overall. I rate the Coros as one of the best sports watches available, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is my favorite sporty smartwatch.

I wore both for my final week of training for the Frankfurt Marathon, and then for race day itself, where I ran 2:25 in my 18th marathon.

With one watch on either wrist, I was keen to see if there were any noticeable differences in their GPS and heart rate accuracy on the day.

I also checked their battery life throughout the weekend to see how fast they were draining, noted any design differences that stood out, and kept in mind how useful they were outside the run itself.

This was a true sports watch vs. smartwatch test, and I’ve picked out the key differences I noticed between the two watches over the marathon weekend below. For more detailed info on either watch, check out our full Apple Watch Ultra 4 review and Coros Pace 4 Pro review.

Before diving into the test, it’s worth noting that the Coros Pace 4 Pro is cheaper than the Apple Watch Ultra 4. It will set you back $449, compared with $799 for the Apple.

Coros rarely reduces its watches, whereas the Ultra 4 is likely to go on sale in time, which will make the gap between them smaller, but the Pace 4 Pro is always going to be the more affordable pick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I love the look of both watches, but they have a different feel on the wrist. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has a full titanium case and is more robust and heavy — it’s a more premium look for sure.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is delightfully light and slim, and has a sapphire crystal case and a titanium bezel, so it’s also going to be durable.

Both watches have three buttons, one of which is a dial, and bright displays that are easy to read in all conditions, including the wet and windy day we had in Frankfurt.

In the rain, the fact that you have to use the touchscreen on the Ultra 4 to navigate its apps and menus is a little annoying compared to the buttons on the Coros.

Importantly, you can do all the key actions you need during runs, like pause and lap, using buttons on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but you have to use the screen to actually end your run.

The Frankfurt Marathon is a tough test for GPS accuracy because the first and final 5K of the race involve twisting around the skyscrapers in the city center. In between, it’s easy enough for watches, with a big loop out to the suburbs.

On the day, the Coros Pace 4 Pro logged a total distance of 42.52km (26.42 miles) and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 logged 43.07km (26.76 miles).

The official marathon distance is 42.19km/ 26.21 miles, and although you never run exactly this distance in an event because of weaving around crowds, I certainly think the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more accurate.

I noticed it was closer in line with the kilometer markers on the course, and because I was in the first 100 runners, I was able to stay pretty close to the most direct racing line throughout the event, so the Ultra 4’s total distance seems too much (it also read long for my colleague Jane at the event).

Looking at the GPS tracks of the watches, you can see they both went wrong at various stages in the city center under the tall buildings there, but the Ultra 4 cut corners and tracked me off the road more often.

This was unexpected for me, as I’ve run marathons with every Apple Watch Ultra and generally they have been pretty good on GPS accuracy in city centers.

I actually used the pacer mode on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it logged me finishing the marathon in 2:23… if only.

Concerning heart rate accuracy, I’m not going to be too hard on either watch because I didn’t wear a chest strap to get a reading to compare them to, and I wore arm sleeves during the marathon, which had watch holes but might have impacted the sensor accuracy.

Looking at the graph of the readings from the two watches, I’d say two things stood out to me when comparing them with past marathons and what I know my heart rate tends to do during them.

One is that the Coros had a consistent reading, but it looks too high compared with my max heart rate of around 176, and it doesn’t trend up throughout the event, which always happens during marathons in my experience.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4’s readings look more accurate to me, aside from the long section from the one-hour to two-hour mark where it didn’t take a reading, greying out the number on the watch because it wasn’t confident it had it right.

I’ve done a lot of testing of the heart rate sensors on both watches outside the marathon (when not wearing arm sleeves), and both are pretty good, but if you want the most reliable results, I’d always say using a chest strap is better.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro certainly wins the battery life battle between these watches, lasting up to seven days on a charge with the screen always-on, compared with 50 hours on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

I used the marathon weekend away as a chance to test the real-world battery life performance of the two, taking both off the charger early Friday morning when I flew to Frankfurt.

After short runs with both watches on Friday and Saturday, the Coros was down to 75% on Sunday morning, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 was at 41% (note that I didn’t sleep with them on, so that saved some battery life).

At that point, I got nervous about the Ultra 4 lasting the marathon and charged it to 75% to match the Coros, which didn’t take long thanks to the fast charging on the Apple.

During the race, I did listen to music on the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for about an hour, which increased how much battery it used, but even so, I could have got by with the 41% it originally had left, as it only drained by 16% in the race.

The Coros only lost 10% of its battery in the race, though, and is certainly the better option for battery life, but the Ultra 4 did impress me over the course of the weekend, and still had 32% of its battery left when I got home on Monday, with only that one short charge over the whole marathon weekend.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is clearly a better smartwatch than the Coros, with a full App Store, easy music storage through streaming services and NFC payments. The Coros can store MP3 files for Bluetooth playback, but that’s about it.

This did come across on a weekend away, where the Ultra 4 could do things like show boarding passes for my flights, and I could wirelessly adjust my running playlist on the watch pre-race and listen to music during the event.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also has more customization options, especially on watch faces. If it’s smarts you want, it’s definitely the better pick.

The weekend trip showcased the pros and cons of both sports watches and smartwatches, and there still isn’t one device from any brand that manages to nail both sides of the coin.

During the marathon, the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more reliable for GPS accuracy and pacing, which is absolutely crucial for me, and it offers much better battery life than the Ultra 4.

However, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is certainly a more useful smartwatch, and it does still offer good sports tracking and a very attractive, robust design.

As someone who has made running most of my job and personality, the superior sports tracking of the Coros Pace 4 Pro is what I’d go for, and I love its lighter design too, but the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a well-rounded pick that handles sports and smarts better than most.

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

I've been training my dad for roughly six years, and one element of his training I've been really ramping up lately? Core work. It's all well and good watching him get stronger, more mobile and better balanced, but a strong core reduces pain, minimizes risk of injury and helps you move well as you age.

There are essential strength exercises in his routine already, but we often work on his core strength at the end of sessions. We try to stay as low-impact as possible, supporting his back while focusing on building deep core stability. My dad has sciatica, so keeping his spine and glutes strong and active is crucial.

As you get better and stronger, you can adapt the load, reps and sets to suit your needs. If you’re ready to get started, check out the three exercises below.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

If you experience limited mobility in your hips, knees, ankles, or spine, go easy and take these exercises slowly. You could progress by adding weight or slowing the exercises down more.

Clamshells strengthen your glutes, which are powerful muscles that help stabilize your pelvis and protect your lower back. Overhead squats require plenty of core stability to help stabilize the weight overhead while you squat. Again, your core works hard to keep your torso upright and stable while carrying a heavy load during the farmer's carry. If you choose to carry one weight, this trains your core for anti-rotation, making you more robust.

If you experience pain, or you're unsure if this exercise is for you due to pregnancy, a health condition, illness, or injury, I recommend seeking medical advice first.

I have my dad hold a weight plate with both hands overhead during overhead squats, but we have been doing this exercise for a long time. You can also wrap a band above your knees and push against it with your legs as you squat. Try to sink your weight into your heels and spread weight to your little and big toes; lift your chest and lower your butt as far as you can.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

During squats, I commonly notice heels rising (thoracic, hip, or ankle-related), knees caving in (often lower-joint-related), backs rounding, or a lack of squat depth. It's better to use your bodyweight first until you improve overall strength and mobility.

Try to keep your spine straight and your shoulders pulled back and down during all exercises, with your core switched and locked on. Imagine bracing for an impact and drawing your breath downward as you move.

#3362. The Teenagers Taking a Cancer Drug to Get Taller

O ne video led to another until eventually my TikTok feed was full of teenagers trying to get taller. They were calling it “heightmaxxing,” a subset of the much-dissected world of “looksmaxxing,” where young men trade strategies for improving their appearance in hopes of warding off a fate of despair and loneliness. For these young men, the logic is mercilessly efficient: Everything in life is better if you’re tall.

The videos arrived with the narrative progression of a course syllabus. First came explainers on “heightism,” or discrimination based on someone’s height. Dating was a frequent point of frustration, with being tall treated as a prerequisite for being considered at all.

Then, slowly but surely, strategies on what you can do about it.

Eventually, I was watching teenagers discuss something called erda. They posted updates on how much they’d grown and compared notes on side effects. Some showed tape measures against marks on a wall; others labeled videos by how many days they’d been taking it. Erda, it turns out, was short for erdafitinib, a cancer drug that the boys on my feed believed could make them taller, pointing to reports of unexpected growth in children being treated for cancer. They were willing to endure debilitating symptoms to find out.

About half an hour into my conversation with Zak, a 17-year-old TikToker in New York, he tells me he had been preparing for the possibility of a hospital stay. He’d been taking erda on and off since he was 15, and after bouts of joint pain and nosebleeds, he expected that something might eventually go wrong. “I was literally saving money every single day. I was putting money aside from my work and everything just for a medical bill from erda.” He says he bought the drug from overseas online vendors, initially paying $300 for a month’s supply.

Zak says height became particularly important to him as he spent more time on social media. He remembers videos of women discussing how tall a man needed to be for them to consider dating them. At school, he says he was made fun of for being shorter than girls in his class. “I don’t like other people towering over me, and I don’t like having to look up to people,” he says. “I don’t know how to put it, but it feels like I’m not in control.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Erdafitinib, sold under the brand name Balversa, was first approved in 2019 to treat certain advanced bladder cancers in adults. Doctors have also used it off-label in clinical trials of children with rare cancers of the central nervous system. The drug’s known side effects are nothing short of gnarly: its prescribing information lists diarrhea, pain in the limbs, nausea, and nails separating from their nail beds, as well as excess phosphate in the blood, which can cause mineral deposits in soft tissues.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Johnson & Johnson, which markets Balversa, expressed concern about online content appearing to show young people using prescription drugs for unapproved purposes or without medical supervision. “It has not been approved to increase height, and its safety and effectiveness have not been established for that purpose or for use in any children or adolescents,” they said, adding that the company urges patients to consult qualified health professionals about treatment and to only use medicines from verified sources under medical supervision.

Zak reports nosebleeds, severely dry skin, and pain that made ordinary movements difficult. “Stretching my arm felt like my wrist was going to tear off,” he says. “Waking up, it felt like my spine was bent. I had to spend one hour of just stretching so my spine feels better.” Even then, he says, the pain persisted.

When we talk, he’s stopped taking the drug, though he’s ultimately pleased with the results and is already thinking about starting again. By his own measurements, he says he grew several inches between roughly ages 15 and 17, while taking erda on and off. He says his height had previously plateaued. Related Content Clavicular Can't Seem to Stay Out of Trouble: A List of His Controversies Are Clavicular’s Followers Rethinking His Influence? I Paid $49 for Clavicular’s ‘Looksmaxxing’ Academy. What I Saw Should Scare Us All Character.ai Was Sued Over a Teen's Suicide. It Just Banned Minors From Chatting With Bots

Adalbert Raimann, a pediatric endocrinologist at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria, is an author of an erdafitinib study often cited by heightmaxxers. Published online in July 2024 in the peer-reviewed journal Hormone Research in Paediatrics, it described unexpected growth in two children with central nervous system tumors.

Raimann explains that, during puberty, growth takes place in cartilage near the ends of bones, known as growth plates. Those plates fuse once we reach our full height, around early adulthood. Erdafitinib blocks proteins called fibroblast growth factor receptors. One of them, FGFR3, normally helps limit bone growth; blocking it can allow growth to speed up while the plates are still active.

Over video chat, Raimann stresses that why those children were receiving the drug matters. Doctors were trying to keep children with rare, life-threatening cancers alive after other treatments had failed. That meant using a drug not approved for children and tolerating serious side effects.

“And those receptors we’re targeting with erda, they’re present in basically every cell,” he says. “So we have no idea, not in adults and especially not in kids in this developing system, what we are doing in five to 10 years.”

After those growth plates have fully closed, Raimann says, there’s no way to naturally grow taller. It’s why some adults in the heightmaxxing world turn to dangerous and excruciating leg-lengthening surgeries, which involve cutting the leg bones and gradually pulling the sections apart so new bone grows in the gaps. It’s also why the demographic hungry for experimental treatments skews so young. The teenagers I spoke with felt like it was potentially their last chance to intervene.

For James, a 17-year-old on the West Coast who asks that I use only his first name, an X-ray helped set off his search for something that could make him taller. During our Zoom call, he holds up a translucent plastic container where he keeps the powder he identifies as erda. Then he brings his hand toward the webcam, curling his fingers to show me his fingernails. They’re yellowish and oozing pus. He says they’ve been falling off. “Bro, it’s bad.”

“I just thought I was just going to be a late bloomer because my uncles and dad, they grew very late,” he says. “So I got a bone-scan X-ray and yo, the doctor said I have a bone age of 18. I can maybe grow another millimeter. And I was five foot five, so it was pretty bad. So then I just knew that there had to be something that could make me taller.”

He says he began taking erda in late August and grew roughly two and a half to three inches in two months, while also using other drugs. “I grew more in two months than I did in one year,” he says.

Erda wasn’t the first drug James had considered. Doctors already prescribe growth hormone to help some children gain height, supplying a hormone the body naturally produces. Andrew Dauber, a pediatric endocrinologist at Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., says there’s a distinction between treating a hormone deficiency and intervening because a child is just short.

“There are children who are deficient in growth hormone, who have severe growth issues, who really medically need growth hormone as indicated. And then there’s this gray zone of using growth hormone for short stature,” he says. The FDA also approves it for some children whose short stature has no identified cause, a category called idiopathic short stature. Dauber describes the threshold as “a height below minus 2.25 standard deviations.” This translates to an adult male height of five feet three and an adult female of four feet 11.

Though guidelines are set by the FDA, doctors have the option of prescribing growth hormone off-label for individuals who they think could benefit from it. The decision involves an expensive treatment with risks, Dauber says, and doctors disagree about when it is warranted.

“I’ve spoken to a lot of pediatric endocrinologists and some say, ‘Listen, I know they’re going to get it. They’re either going to get it off the internet or they’re going to go see a doctor who doesn’t know as much about it, and I feel like I should just give it to them and at least monitor them for safety and do it in a safer way,’” he says. “And then there are many endocrinologists who feel like this is not really a disease or not really a medical problem.”

Dauber says he has now received his first patient inquiry about erda. He will not prescribe it for growth. “That’s way too dangerous. We only know about it at the chemotherapeutic doses,” he says, referring to the amounts used to treat cancer.

James says that when he was younger, his parents refused to let him take growth hormone. After an endocrinologist told him he was nearly done growing at five foot five, he says, their guilt over that decision made them more permissive about his experiments with erda and other drugs. “They kind of let me do everything,” he says.

Zak says his parents “don’t approve of anything I’m doing.”

Both say that nothing would stop them from trying anything they can to get taller. “There’s this life that I have in mind, and I just want it so badly that I’m not going to let some risk stop me from getting the life I want,” James says. “I don’t know. I just want it so badly.”

There’s been a marked turn toward DIY healthcare in recent years, as alternative medicine and biohacking protocols gain mainstream popularity. People on social media increasingly promote injectable peptides and other invasive methods for optimizing one’s health and looks. For Zak, the adverse reactions have become part of that pursuit. “If I get into side effects, nobody would want to touch this compound,” he says. “But to me, I get obsessed over this stuff, and I still think it was worth it.”

James calls his bedroom a lab. He says he sources the drugs through black-market online suppliers. In addition to erda and human growth hormone, he says he’s experimented with tamoxifen and letrozole, two drugs used to treat breast cancer, and abaloparatide, a drug for osteoporosis. He also uses experimental compounds called SAG 21K and KY19382, which researchers have studied in mice for their effects on bone repair or growth.

He says he went to the hospital with a stomach bleed during his first month of taking erda, though he isn’t sure which exact compound caused it. He has since switched to online school because he says the pain and vomiting made attending in person too difficult. “At school, I threw up blood one time,” he says. “And it hurt so bad to move. I can only go out once a week. I just go out on Fridays and just rest the whole day because everything I’m doing, it makes me so tired and hungry that I literally just have to lay down.” He says his bones feel like they’re stretching apart. “So it’s hard to do anything.”

The anxiety around male height isn’t exclusively coming from the teens themselves. Both Raimann and Dauber say they regularly see parents looking for ways to help their child reach a particular height, especially the parents of young boys. “I had a mother say in front of her child, her teenage son, ‘If he ends up five-seven, his life is over,’” Dauber recalls. “My eyes just shot open, and I’m like, ‘Well, think about the psychological effect that that has on your teenage child to say such a thing.’”

“I think there’s an enormous social pressure, especially on young males to become taller,” Raimann says. He says some boys perceive the risk of remaining short as greater than the risk of taking experimental drugs.

Zak explains why he feels he has to keep improving. “I’m trying to maximize every aspect of my body. No matter what I do, I still feel like it’s not enough,” he says. And when it comes to girls, he says, “They constantly want something better.”

Across social media, short men lament poor treatment romantically, pointing to research on the advantages taller men enjoy both professionally and in dating. On Reddit, communities like r/short and r/shortguys draw tens of thousands of members sharing their experiences. One user, who says he is a 21-year-old in Spain, tells me in a DM that reassuring stories about other short men did little to change his outlook.

“People know how a short person is treated in this world; the problem is they try to turn a blind eye. They play dumb, saying things like: ‘Well, but I know someone who…’ — purely anecdotal experiences that honestly don’t reflect the reality for the majority.”

For all of the recent talk of short kings in pop culture, the men I spoke with describe familiar stigmas around male height.

Jason Nagata, a pediatrician specializing in adolescent and young adult medicine who treats patients with eating disorders, recently heard through consultations about a patient asking to use erda to try to get taller. Nagata says the repetition of certain types of content can distort a young person’s sense of how common these practices are.

“I do think that social media and online communities normalize behaviors that might otherwise seem extreme,” Nagata says. “So if you’re constantly seeing peers or influencers discussing hormones, drugs, steroids, or surgery as sort of ordinary optimization tools, then it makes it seem like everyone’s doing that.” A young man who engages with this content gets more of it in his feed, he says. “So I think you can have a misperception of what’s normal.”

Nagata says that one way to help dissuade this kind of behavior is to hear kids out. “When talking with teens about height or other appearance concerns, I recommend starting with open-ended, nonjudgmental conversations,” he adds. “Parents can lead with curiosity and try to understand what their child is concerned about, what they hope to achieve, and what they have heard or seen online. Once you understand where they’re coming from, you’re in a better position to provide helpful, evidence-based guidance.”

Zak says he first started looking into steroids and looksmaxxing drugs when he was 12. He remembers a teacher catching him researching performance-enhancing drugs on his school Chromebook. “My friend has a video of my teacher yelling at me,” he says.

The pandemic put his interest in pharmacology into overdrive, as he was able to spend hours online doing research. “I have photos of my screen time. It’s literally 17 hours of YouTube videos on this stuff,” he says of the period. “I was obsessed. I forgot to eat my meals.” He tells me he even performed nipple-reduction surgery on himself after using YouTube to watch surgical procedures.

Asked why he shares his experiments online, Zak says, “I just want to show other people how it’s so possible to literally do anything.” He describes commenters under his erda posts announcing that their own orders will arrive in a few weeks and asking whether the side effects are as bad as they sound. He says he does not sell erdafitinib or give out his source. He also thinks the size of an online audience can give a misleading impression of how many people are actually taking it.

“You would think that there’s a lot of people, but that’s just because having a platform helps you reach so many people.”

A TikTok U.S. spokesperson says the platform prohibits content promoting erda or showing its use, as part of its rules against selling or facilitating access to regulated or high-risk goods. The spokesperson says TikTok may limit search results for unapproved or potentially unsafe products and direct users to authoritative health resources, and that the company continually refines those measures.

Many of the accounts I’d initially seen have since been banned. Right after our interview, Zak sent me an email letting me know his account had been banned, pointing me to his new backup username.

Beyond social platforms, the search for drugs leads to gray-market vendors. Zak tells me he lost money twice trying to buy another compound using Bitcoin. One of his suppliers, he says, worked at a biotech lab.

“I went on a Chinese dating app in a certain city in China that’s known for its biotech labs and things like that,” he says. The woman he met there sent him research chemicals and could even supply custom compounds, he says.

Tim Mackey, whose company S3 Research monitors online drug markets, had his analysts look into erdafitinib after I contacted him. They found discussions on Telegram and other platforms about sourcing and taking the drug. Some people appeared to be buying raw ingredients rather than a finished medicine. Mackey says buyers cannot assume they are getting what is advertised.

“Cancer drugs tend to be in a very controlled supply chain,” he says. What buyers find online could be legitimate medicine diverted from that chain, raw pharmaceutical ingredients not intended for human use, or counterfeit products.

Dauber cautions that the published reports of children growing on erda also describe abnormal bone growth and development. Even so, the warnings haven’t deterred Zak or James. Both say they’re treated better by their peers now that they’re taller. Zak says critics in his comments tell him that he’s trying to die early by taking experimental compounds, but he insists the opposite. He wants to live his life fully and believes the drugs can help him do that. James tells me he is scared of dying and worries about cancer each time he takes a new untested substance. He also says another hospital stay wouldn’t persuade him to stop; he wants to keep going until he reaches a height he is happy with. Somewhere around six foot four. I ask what he imagines life would feel like at that height.

“I don’t know. I feel like I wouldn’t have to worry about anything really, because my entire life, everything that’s made me sad and depressed and just not doing OK, it all stems from just my looks and being insecure, all of that,” he says. “So if I fix everything, almost all my problems would go away. When you’re six-four and you look perfect, your perfect face, perfect everything.”

If you love watching hummingbirds visit your yard, you may wonder whether to keep your hummingbird feeder filled with nectar through the winter or take it down until spring.

My initial thought was that keeping a hummingbird feeder up through the colder months would stop these beautiful birds from migrating, but is this really true?

During the summer, hummingbirds can be spotted across North America, but most head south to migrate after the breeding season.

I assumed hummingbirds migrate to find rich-nectar flowers and tiny insects that keep them fuelled, but the truth has more to do with daylight.

Hunger alone doesn’t make them fly south. Their internal biological clocks recognize changes in daylight hours, triggering hormonal shifts that drive them south. Only those not strong enough to make the flight get left behind.

While most of these tiny creatures fly south to warmer climes in Mexico or Central America, some stay behind. According to the American Bird Conservancy, Anna’s Hummingbirds tend to remain along parts of the West Coast, while you might spot the Ruby-throated Hummingbird across certain sections of southern Florida.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Photoperiodism is how hummingbirds, and other living plants and animals, react to changes in daylight hours. According to ScienceDirect, shifting daylight cues trigger seasonal behaviors like bird migration.

Healthy hummingbirds will head south as daylight hours decrease, but strugglers will hold back. Leaving your feeder out for two more weeks after their fellows have flown can help them catch up and build the strength to migrate. It can also act as fuelling stations for those who have already taken flight, and want to swoop in for a feed.

If you decide to keep your hummingbird feeder up in winter, taking good care of it and replenishing the food regularly will help these tiny creatures survive. When other food sources like nectar and insects are harder to find, they will rely on your familiar spot for nourishment.

Why have one hummingbird feeder when you can have two? This double pack contains 5 feeding ports on each feeder, as well as a built-in ant guard, circular perch, wide mouth and easy-to-fill base.

A drop in temperature changes how you maintain your hummingbird feeder, rather than whether you should take it down. According to Pops Birding, nectar at the standard 1: 4 ratio — that’s one part white sugar to four parts water — freezes a little below the freezing point of cold water.

So, when the temperature gets chilly, you can either bring your feeder in at night to keep it from freezing or run two on rotation so one is always thawed.

Your hummingbird feeder also needs to be kept clean, as nectar residue is a breeding ground for mold and bacteria. When pouring fresh nectar into your feeder, clean it out first, and change the nectar every 2-3 days in normal conditions, in winter it can go a few more days. However, if it looks cloudy or you spot visible mold, Pop’s Birding recommends cleaning your feeder and replacing the nectar immediately.

Between flights, lodgings, activities, and packing lists, there’s a lot to consider — and pay for— when it comes to planning a trip abroad. Your cell phone plan shouldn’t be one of them.

Many travelers have learned the hard way that certain cell phone plans can kill your wallet with roaming charges come the end of a trip. This is because your home carrier essentially rents network access from foreign providers if you switch on your data, make a call, or send a text in another country.

However, if you travel often, you don’t need to deal with massive roaming charges at the end of every trip abroad. Certain carriers offer wireless plans with large international data packages included, which means you won’t need to worry about purchasing an international pass or an eSIM while planning your trip. Just touch down and continue using your phone (and your own number) like you would at home.

Ahead are three of the best wireless plans for traveling abroad, including options from T-Mobile, Google Fi, and Verizon.

One of the best cell phone plans for international travel is T-Mobile’s Experience Beyond 2.0 plan. The premium cell package offers unlimited text and 15 gigabytes of high-speed data in more than 215 countries and destinations — all without requiring a separate pass or payment. If you’re traveling to Mexico or Canada, you’ll get 30 gigabytes of data. Once you hit that data cap, you’ll still be able to access the internet, but speeds will slow down a bit. The Experience Beyond plan also comes with other travel perks like hotel and rental car discounts, cruise credits, and even a complimentary drink on Delta flights. If you’re flying on Delta, Alaska, Hawaiian, or Southwest airlines, you’ll also get free in-flight Wi-Fi.T-Mobile’s Experience More package is also good for travelers, offering 5 gigabytes of high-speed data in more than 215 countries and destinations and 15 in Mexico and Canada.

Google Fi Unlimited Premium is also a great choice for any travelers going abroad. You get 50 gigabytes of data in 200+ destinations before speeds slow down. All roaming data is included in your plan, so you don’t need a pass and won’t get slapped with a surprise bill after returning home. You’ll also get unlimited texting, and calls cost about 20 cents a minute.Another thing we like about the Google Fi plan is that you get 500 gigabytes of hotspot tethering. This is great for any travel (domestic or international) where you need to use your laptop or tablet where there’s no WiFi available.

Verizon’s Unlimited Ultimate package is another cell plan worth considering for staying connected while abroad. While traveling internationally in more than 210 countries, you get unlimited talk (which the packages above don’t offer) and text, and 15 gigabytes of data before speeds are reduced.

#3353. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3351. Channel 4 Cancels ‘Married At First Sight UK’ After Rape Allegations

Channel 4 has canceled Married at First Sight UK (MAFS UK) following two external reviews into welfare on the show that was hit by rape allegations earlier this year.

Despite one review saying “it would be reasonable to continue producing future series,” Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra said MAFS UK has now “run its course.” Neither the current sixth season, which had been filmed, or spin-off Second Marriage at First Sight, which was due to roll cameras over the summer, will air. The previous five seasons will remain absent from Channel 4’s VoD player, although other versions from around the world are available to watch including Married at First Sight U.S. Related Stories News 'The Cube' Creator Adam Adler Joins Channel 4's Production Biz As Creative Director News Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK

“The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over ten years,” said Dogra, who was mere weeks into the job when the MAFS UK scandal erupted. “Channel 4 has always thrived on reinvention and this is a moment to kickstart a new era of creative renewal, using the considerable budget to find the next generation of distinctive and disruptive British television.” Watch on Deadline

The reviews were commissioned after BBC News published allegations from two women who alleged they were raped by partners they met on the show, while another claimed she was victim of a non-consensual sex act. The three men accused of wrongdoing all deny the accusations. One cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape over the summer.

While Channel 4 said the specific allegations “remain a matter for the relevant authorities,” the first review from legal firm Clyde & Co examined welfare protocols on MAFS UK and whether regulator Ofcom’s code was breached. The second, conducted by ex-BBC One boss Lorraine Heggessey, looked into whether changes should be made to protocols for MAFS UK to strengthen contributor welfare in the future. Separately, Ofcom opened its own investigation in July.

Rules broken around “prohibited substances”

Clyde & Co’s review found Channel 4 and producer CPL Productions had not breached the Ofcom code.

It did, however, “identify a small number of instances in which the show’s established protocols had not been fully applied.”

These, it said, related to contributors breaking the rules around “prohibited substances.” These contributors were given a “first and final warning” rather than “being removed from the progamme,” according to the review.

Clyde & Co, which examined more than 30,000 documents, 20 hours of broadcast and unbroadcast footage and conducted 15 interviews, said CPL and Channel 4 could have “undertaken a more structured longer-term review over multiple series so that any further tightening of processes and procedures could be made in response to a more holistic and long-term assessment.”

Heggessey’s forward-facing review, meanwhile, suggested Channel 4 could make more MAFS UK with various welfare tweaks, although Dogra, who once again said today she is “very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt,” came to a different view.

Notably, Heggessey said that while “the complexity of the production” requires “significant oversight from Channel 4,” the network’s involvement has “at times led to a lack of objective scrutiny over some production decisions.”

Heggessey’s recommendations included separate bedrooms on couples’ wedding nights and honeymoons before giving them the option to “opt in” to sharing a room, reviewing the frequency with which they are asked about the physical side of their relationship by the production team and reducing the number of couples per series.

Within the couples’ apartments, Heggessey suggested Channel 4 could install CCTV, use individual safe words and panic buttons, and provide lockable ensuite bathrooms.

She also suggested various tweaks to casting including “undertaking psychological testing and profiling of final contributors in person rather than via video call,” alongside considering whether psychological assessments should “take into account current societal trends” like misogyny and attitudes to consent.

As it stands, these recommendations will not be taken up as the show has been axed. Instead, new Channel 4 programs chief David Brindley, who begins in January, will be looking after MAFS UK’s reallocated budget.

“MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production,” said Dogra. “I am grateful to everyone at Channel 4 and CPL Productions who has worked on the show and want to thank them for their significant efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, something which was recognised in both reviews. I hope our actions – in swiftly commissioning the review and taking clear, decisive steps – demonstrate our commitment to the wellbeing of all contributors and our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards.”

A CPL statement said the indie “understands Channel 4’s decision to bring MAFS to an end.” “The independent reviews gave CPL the opportunity to discuss in depth the welfare processes already in place and that the Heggessey review found that ‘the welfare protocols for MAFS UK were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard from which other productions in the industry have learnt’,” read the statement. “CPL has always put contributor welfare at the heart of its programme making and will continue to do so. CPL have worked closely with Channel 4 for many years and throughout the review process, and we look forward to working with them again in the future.”

MAFS, which originated in Denmark 13 years ago, remains huge in several territories, with the American, Australian and New Zealand versions all still available on Channel 4’s VoD player. The U.S. version airs on Peacock.

Across a decade, MAFS UK has been a huge hit for Channel 4, moreso when the format was tweaked in 2021 to bring it more in line with other versions like the popular Australian one.

The MAFS UK reviews were at least the third set of external reviews launched by Channel 4 over the past decade, following one into the suicide of true crime producer John Balson and another into the behavior of Escape to the Chateau hosts Dick and Angel Strawbridge. The Balson review found that Channel 4 had acted “reasonably and appropriately” with its duty of care before the producer took his own life. Channel 4 cut ties with the Strawbridges after that review.
